children.title: Sources of Mixed-Integer Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Structural origins of nonconvex geometry in mixed-integer nonlinear models.

children.title: Continuous Nonconvexity with Discrete Design
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex continuous geometry that remains after discrete decisions are fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Nonconvexity with Discrete Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines residual continuous nonconvexity after fixing the discrete design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a mixed-integer feasible set \(F=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:g_j(x,y)\le 0,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\). Continuous nonconvexity with discrete design is present if there exists \(\bar y\in Y\) for which the fiber \(F_{\bar y}=\{x\in X:(x,\bar y)\in F\}\) is nonconvex, or the restricted objective \(x\mapsto f(x,\bar y)\) is nonconvex on \(F_{\bar y}\). Thus fixing every integer variable does not necessarily reduce the model to a convex continuous optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous nonconvexity remains when some fixed discrete design yields a nonconvex continuous feasible fiber or a nonconvex restricted objective.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\).
The functions \(f\) and \(g_j\) are defined on \(X\times Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For some \(\bar y\in Y\), either \(F_{\bar y}\) or \(f(\cdot,\bar y)\) on that fiber is nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Continuous feasible fiber associated with fixed discrete design \(\bar y\).

children.title: Integer-Activated Nonlinear Structure
children.top_down_role: Nonlinear terms or domains controlled by discrete alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Activated Nonlinear Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines nonlinear constraints or terms enabled by discrete alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y_k\in\{0,1\}\) select an alternative and let \(h_k:D_k\to\mathbb R^{q_k}\) be nonlinear. An integer-activated nonlinear structure imposes the implication \(y_k=1\Rightarrow x\in D_k\) and \(h_k(x)\le 0\), while the corresponding restriction is absent when \(y_k=0\). More generally, for finite \(Y\), each assignment \(y\in Y\) may select its own domain \(D_y\), nonlinear mapping \(h_y\), or expression graph. The feasible set is consequently a union of assignment-specific nonlinear regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete assignment activates a nonlinear expression, constraint, or domain that need not apply under other assignments.
assumptions_latex: Each activated mapping \(h_k\) is defined on its associated domain \(D_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The active continuous feasible region depends on the selected integer assignment.

notation.meaning: Domain and nonlinear mapping selected by alternative \(k\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical formulation is plausible, but the cited general model-structure section does not reliably support the specialized implication-based activation definition or assignment-specific expression graphs. An authoritative disjunctive or mixed-integer nonlinear modeling source is required.

children.title: Discrete–Continuous Product Structure
children.top_down_role: Products coupling discrete and continuous variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete–Continuous Product Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the exact lifted representation of bounded binary–continuous products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(y\in\{0,1\}\), \(L\le x\le U\), and introduce \(w=yx\). The product graph is represented exactly by \[L y\le w\le U y,\qquad x-U(1-y)\le w\le x-L(1-y).\] If \(y=0\), these inequalities force \(w=0\); if \(y=1\), they force \(w=x\). Hence the displayed linear system, together with binary \(y\) and finite bounds on \(x\), is an exact mixed-integer representation of the discrete–continuous product. Relaxing \(y\) to \([0,1]\) gives the convex hull over the bounded box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded binary–continuous product has an exact four-inequality lifted formulation; its continuous relaxation is the product graph’s convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(-\infty<L\le x\le U<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four inequalities are equivalent to \(w=yx\), and with \(0\le y\le1\) describe its convex hull.

notation.meaning: Finite lower and upper bounds on \(x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four inequalities and convex-hull claim are standard for a bounded binary–continuous product, but the exactness and hull assertions are nontrivial and have no cited source.

children.title: Nonconvex Disjunctive Geometry
children.top_down_role: Unions of nonlinear feasible regions induced by logical or integer choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Disjunctive Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the union geometry induced by discrete nonlinear alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be finite and let \(F_k=\{x\in D_k:g_{ki}(x)\le0,\ i=1,\ldots,m_k\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) denote the continuous region selected by alternative \(k\). The associated disjunctive feasible set is \(F=\bigcup_{k\in K}F_k\), equivalently \(x\in F_k\) for at least one selected alternative. Its geometry is nonconvex whenever there exist \(x^a\in F_r\), \(x^b\in F_s\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\) such that \(\lambda x^a+(1-\lambda)x^b\notin F\), even if every individual \(F_k\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete alternatives create a union of continuous feasible regions, which can be nonconvex even when each individual region is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is finite.
Each \(F_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the feasible region of one discrete alternative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The induced continuous projection is \(F=\bigcup_{k\in K}F_k\), with nonconvexity characterized by failure to contain a chord.

notation.meaning: Finite index set of discrete alternatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the finite-composition representation assumption and its explicit representation boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(f\) and every constraint function \(g_j\) are assumed factorable: each is computable in finitely many steps from model variables and real constants using supported unary operators, such as \(\log,\exp,\sin,\cos,\tan\), and binary operators, such as \(+,-,\times,/,\widehat{\ }\). Functions supplied only as black boxes or through representations outside this finite operator calculus, including the indefinite-integral example cited in the extract, are excluded from the framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each objective and constraint function must be exposed as a finite expression built from variables, constants, and supported operators. Black-box functions and representations outside this expression calculus are excluded.
assumptions_latex: f,g_j\text{ are constructed from model variables and real constants by finitely many supported unary and binary operations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ and every }g_j\text{ admit factorable finite-expression representations in the stated operator calculus.}

children.title: Smooth Factorable MINLP
children.top_down_role: Factorable models composed of smooth primitives.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Factorable MINLP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines factorable MINLPs built from differentiable elemental operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth factorable MINLP has variables \((x,y)\in X\times Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^p\) and objective and constraint functions representable by finite acyclic expression graphs. Every leaf is a variable or constant, and every internal node applies an arithmetic operation or an elemental function to earlier nodes. On an open neighborhood of the relevant bounded domain, each primitive is continuously differentiable and every intermediate value lies in its primitive's domain. The resulting functions may be nonconvex despite their smooth factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth factorable MINLP expresses every objective and constraint through finite graphs of differentiable elemental operations, while allowing global nonconvexity.
assumptions_latex: The relevant continuous domain \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is bounded.
All intermediate expressions remain inside the domains of their primitives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each model function admits a finite continuously differentiable expression graph on the relevant domain.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expression-graph description is plausible, but boundedness is not generally intrinsic to the definition of a smooth factorable MINLP. The cited general model-structure section does not establish this particular definition or its smoothness conditions.

children.title: Nonsmooth Piecewise-Factorable Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Factorable models containing nonsmooth or piecewise-defined primitives.

children.title: Nonsmooth Factorable Primitives
children.top_down_role: Factorable primitives whose local behavior lacks smoothness.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Factorable Primitives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines admissible nonsmooth nodes in a factorable expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonsmooth factorable primitive is a finite-arity mapping \(\phi:D\subseteq\mathbb R^r\to\mathbb R\) that can appear as one node of a finite expression graph and is not differentiable everywhere on \(D\). Typical primitives include \(\lvert u\rvert\), \(\max\{u,v\}\), and \(\min\{u,v\}\). Its switching set is \(S_\phi=\{z\in D:\phi\text{ is not differentiable at }z\}\). A factorable expression containing such a node is nonsmooth at any input whose evaluated intermediate argument belongs to \(S_\phi\), unless composition causes cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth factorable primitive is an expression-graph operation, such as absolute value or maximum, whose differentiability fails on a switching set.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^r\) is the primitive's domain.
The primitive is evaluable as a finite-arity expression-graph node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonsmoothness can occur when an evaluated intermediate argument reaches \(S_\phi\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primitive and switching-set formulation is mathematically coherent and fits the leaf, but no authoritative source supports the chosen factorability terminology or composition qualification.

children.title: Piecewise-Factorable Expressions
children.top_down_role: Factorable expressions assembled from explicit piecewise regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Factorable Expressions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines expressions assembled from finitely many factorable regime formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be covered by finitely many regions \(D_1,\ldots,D_K\), and let each \(f_k:D_k\to\mathbb R\) be factorable. A function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise factorable if \(f(x)=f_k(x)\) whenever \(x\in D_k\), with coincident values \(f_k(x)=f_\ell(x)\) on every overlap where both regimes apply. If a priority or selection rule is specified instead, that rule must assign exactly one value on overlaps. The expression may be nonsmooth or discontinuous across regime boundaries even when every \(f_k\) is smooth in its region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-factorable expression selects among finitely many factorable formulas on specified regions, with overlap rules ensuring a single value.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\bigcup_{k=1}^K D_k\) with finite \(K\).
Every regime formula \(f_k\) is factorable on \(D_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime formulas and overlap rule define a single-valued function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-regime construction is coherent, including its overlap rule, but the proposed definition of piecewise factorability has no cited authoritative source.

children.title: Cross-Regime Relaxation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Relaxation issues arising where piecewise regimes meet.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Relaxation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies why separately valid regime relaxations may fail across their union.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=F_1\cup F_2\) and suppose \(R_k\supseteq F_k\) is a valid relaxation for each regime. Using both regime relaxations simultaneously, as \(R_1\cap R_2\), is generally invalid because a point in \(F_1\setminus R_2\) or \(F_2\setminus R_1\) may be removed. Using \(R_1\cup R_2\) is valid but remains disjunctive, while replacing it by \(\operatorname{conv}(R_1\cup R_2)\) is a valid convex relaxation that can admit cross-regime chord points not in \(F\). Thus regime-validity does not imply global validity under intersection, nor tightness after convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate regime relaxations cannot generally be intersected; their convexified union is valid but may introduce spurious points between regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(F_k\subseteq R_k\) for \(k\in\{1,2\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\cap R_2\) need not contain \(F\), whereas \(\operatorname{conv}(R_1\cup R_2)\) contains \(F\) but may be loose.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-inclusion observations are correct and the failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf, but the cross-regime validity and convexification claims lack any source.

children.title: Integer-Dependent Expression Graphs
children.top_down_role: Expression graphs whose active structure or domains depend on discrete decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Dependent Expression Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines expression graphs whose topology or node domains depend on integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) be finite. An integer-dependent expression graph is a family \(\{G_y:y\in Y\}\) of finite acyclic graphs such that assignment \(y\) selects the active nodes, arcs, primitive operations, or intermediate domains used to evaluate a model function \(f(x,y)\). For every feasible \((x,y)\), evaluation must follow \(G_y\) in topological order and every intermediate value must lie in the selected primitive's domain. Distinct assignments may therefore yield different factorizations or even different domains for the same modeled output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integer assignment selects an expression graph’s active nodes, operations, links, or domains, producing an assignment-specific evaluation rule.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\) is finite.
Every selected graph \(G_y\) is finite and acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each feasible assignment \(y\) determines a well-defined graph evaluation of \(f(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Expression graph selected by integer assignment \(y\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed family-of-graphs definition is specialized and is not supported by the cited general section. Requiring the integer assignment set to be finite also unnecessarily excludes otherwise meaningful integer-dependent expression graphs.

children.title: Indefinite Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programming
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models with indefinite quadratic objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Mixed-Integer Quadratic Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines MIQP with a nonconvex indefinite quadratic objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite mixed-integer quadratic program has the form \[\min\left\{\tfrac12 z^\top Qz+c^\top z:Az\le b,\ z_i\in\mathbb Z\ \text{for }i\in I,\ z_j\in\mathbb R\ \text{for }j\notin I\right\},\] where \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) has at least one negative eigenvalue. Consequently the quadratic objective is not convex on \(\mathbb R^n\). Relative to the feasible affine hull, nonconvexity is effective only if a feasible continuous direction \(d\) satisfies \(d^\top Qd<0\); otherwise the restricted objective may still be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite MIQP has linear constraints, mixed-integer variables, and a quadratic objective with negative curvature relevant to feasible continuous directions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\).
\(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) identifies integer coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A negative eigenvalue makes the objective nonconvex globally; feasible negative curvature makes that nonconvexity effective on the model domain.

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section concerns indefinite quadratic problems but does not clearly support the mixed-integer extension. Moreover, a 'feasible continuous direction' is not defined precisely enough to establish effective nonconvexity on a mixed-integer feasible domain.

children.title: Nonconvex MIQCP
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models with nonconvex quadratic constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex MIQCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines mixed-integer quadratically constrained models with nonconvex quadratic geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer quadratically constrained program has objective \(\tfrac12 z^\top Q_0z+c_0^\top z\) and constraints \(\tfrac12 z^\top Q_kz+c_k^\top z\le b_k\) for \(k=1,\ldots,m\), together with bounds, linear constraints, and integrality on coordinates indexed by \(I\). It is a nonconvex MIQCP when the objective has feasible negative curvature or at least one quadratic constraint defines a nonconvex sublevel set on the continuous domain; a sufficient global test is that \(Q_0\not\succeq0\) or some \(Q_k\not\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex MIQCP combines integer restrictions with a quadratic objective or quadratic constraint exhibiting relevant negative curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_k\in\mathbb S^n\) for \(k=0,\ldots,m\).
Coordinates in \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) are integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Negative curvature in the objective or a quadratic constraint can make the MIQCP nonconvex on its continuous domain.

notation.meaning: Symmetric Hessian matrix of quadratic expression \(k\).

source_refs.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2 Large Scale Indefinite Quadratic Problems p. 247

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claim that any non-positive-semidefinite constraint matrix is a sufficient global test for a nonconvex MIQCP is false without conditions on the right-hand side and domain; an indefinite quadratic sublevel set can still be convex or vacuous after restriction. The cited indefinite-objective section also does not support the quadratic-constraint extension.

children.title: Binary-Activated Quadratic Structure
children.top_down_role: Quadratic structure dominated or activated by binary variables.

children.title: Binary Quadratic Structure
children.top_down_role: Quadratic interactions involving binary variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Quadratic Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the canonical polynomial representation of quadratic binary interactions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(y\in\{0,1\}^p\), a binary quadratic function is \(q(y)=c+\sum_{i=1}^p a_i y_i+\sum_{1\le i<j\le p}b_{ij}y_i y_j\). Because \(y_i^2=y_i\), every quadratic polynomial in binary variables has this form after absorbing diagonal terms into the linear coefficients. Introducing \(w_{ij}=y_i y_j\), each product is represented exactly by \[0\le w_{ij},\qquad w_{ij}\le y_i,\qquad w_{ij}\le y_j,\qquad w_{ij}\ge y_i+y_j-1.\] Thus a pure binary quadratic expression admits an exact mixed-integer linear lifting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary idempotence removes square terms, and every remaining pairwise product has an exact four-inequality linear lifting.
assumptions_latex: A lifted variable \(w_{ij}\) is introduced for each retained pairwise product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted linear system is equivalent to \(w_{ij}=y_i y_j\) for binary \(y_i,y_j\).

children.title: On–Off Quadratic Activation
children.top_down_role: Quadratic terms controlled by discrete activation states.

knowledge_statements.title: On–Off Quadratic Activation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive representation of a quadratic term activated by one binary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\), \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+a^{\mathsf T}x+b\). An on–off quadratic epigraph is the disjunction
\[
\bigl(z=0,\ x=0,\ t\geq 0\bigr)\quad\lor\quad\bigl(z=1,\ x\in X,\ t\geq q(x)\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, the binary state suppresses the participating continuous variables when off and enforces the quadratic epigraph when on. Bounds linking \(x\) to \(z\), such as \(\ell z\leq x\leq uz\), encode the required condition \(z=0\Rightarrow x=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The off state forces participating variables to zero; the on state enforces the specified quadratic epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(0\in X\).
\(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=0\Rightarrow(x=0,t\geq0)\) and \(z=1\Rightarrow(t\geq q(x))\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Structure of Global Optimization Models p. 3

children.title: Indicator-Controlled Quadratic Terms
children.top_down_role: Indicator representations for conditionally active quadratic expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator-Controlled Quadratic Terms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical activation of a quadratic constraint without requiring variables to vanish in the inactive state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and let \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+a^{\mathsf T}x+b\) on \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). An indicator-controlled quadratic constraint has the form
\[
z=1\ \Longrightarrow\ q(x)\leq0.
\]
Its feasible set is
\[
\bigl(\{0\}\times X\bigr)\ \cup\ \bigl(\{1\}\times\{x\in X:q(x)\leq0\}\bigr).
\]
Thus the quadratic restriction is imposed in the indicated state, while the inactive state retains every point of \(X\); reversing the roles of zero and one gives the complementary convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator value activates a quadratic constraint; in the inactive state, the quadratic restriction is absent.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\{0,1\}\) and \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
\(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=(\{0\}\times X)\cup(\{1\}\times\{x\in X:q(x)\leq0\})\).

children.title: Sparse Low-Rank Quadratic Geometry
children.top_down_role: Quadratic structure supporting sparsity- or rank-aware relaxations.

children.title: Sparse Quadratic Interaction Graphs
children.top_down_role: Quadratic structures with limited variable interaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Quadratic Interaction Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation and quantitative sparsity measure for pairwise interactions in a symmetric quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(q(x)=x^{\mathsf T}Qx+a^{\mathsf T}x+b\), where \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R\), the quadratic interaction graph is the undirected graph \(G_Q=(V,E)\) defined by
\[
V=\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad E=\bigl\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j\leq n,\ Q_{ij}\neq0\bigr\}.
\]
Its off-diagonal interaction sparsity is measured by \(|E|\), or equivalently by the edge density \(2|E|/[n(n-1)]\) when \(n\geq2\). Diagonal coefficients represent unary square terms and do not create edges under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variables are vertices, nonzero quadratic cross coefficients create edges, and graph sparsity is quantified by the number or density of those edges.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\).
\(Q\in\mathbb S^n\), \(a\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(b\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{i,j\}\in E\Longleftrightarrow 1\leq i<j\leq n\text{ and }Q_{ij}\neq0\).

notation.meaning: set of nonzero off-diagonal quadratic interactions

children.title: Low-Rank Quadratic Forms
children.top_down_role: Quadratic forms governed by reduced spectral dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Quadratic Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral factor representation of a symmetric low-rank quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) have rank \(r\). There exist nonzero eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r\) and orthonormal vectors \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\) such that
\[
Q=\sum_{k=1}^r\lambda_k u_ku_k^{\mathsf T},\qquad x^{\mathsf T}Qx=\sum_{k=1}^r\lambda_k(u_k^{\mathsf T}x)^2.
\]
Equivalently, writing \(U=[u_1\ \cdots\ u_r]\) and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r)\), one has \(Q=UDU^{\mathsf T}\). The quadratic geometry therefore depends on only \(r\) linear projections of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r symmetric quadratic form is a signed sum of squares of r linear projections.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{\mathsf T}Qx=\sum_{k=1}^r\lambda_k(u_k^{\mathsf T}x)^2\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: orthonormal eigenvector of the quadratic matrix

children.title: Sparsity–Rank Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where sparsity or rank most strongly influences relaxation design.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity–Rank Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete families showing that matrix sparsity and low rank do not imply one another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sparsity and rank are independent structural measures. For any \(n\geq2\), the diagonal matrix \(Q=I_n\) has no off-diagonal interaction edges but satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=n\). Conversely, if \(u\in\mathbb R^n\) has every component nonzero, then \(Q=uu^{\mathsf T}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{rank}(Q)=1\), while every off-diagonal entry \(Q_{ij}=u_i u_j\) is nonzero and its interaction graph is complete. Hence neither sparse interaction nor low rank alone entails the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal full-rank and dense rank-one matrices show that interaction sparsity and low rank are logically independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_{I_n}\text{ is edgeless with rank }n\), whereas \(G_{uu^{\mathsf T}}\text{ is complete with rank }1\).

children.title: Mixed-Integer Polynomial Optimization
children.top_down_role: Polynomial mixed-integer models handled through factorable or algebraic relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Polynomial Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional polynomial optimization with continuous and integer decision components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n,q\in\mathbb N\) with \(q\geq1\), let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite index sets, and let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q\). A mixed-integer polynomial optimization problem has the form
\[
\inf\bigl\{p_0(x,y):p_i(x,y)\leq0\ (i\in I),\ p_j(x,y)=0\ (j\in J),\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\bigr\},
\]
where \(p_0\) and every constraint function \(p_i\) and \(p_j\) are real multivariate polynomials in \((x,y)\). Thus the model combines polynomial algebraic expressions with an explicit nonempty-dimensional integer decision block.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer polynomial optimization problem has polynomial objective and constraint functions and at least one integer-restricted decision component.
assumptions_latex: \(n,q\in\mathbb N\) and \(q\geq1\).
\(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), and \(I,J\) are finite index sets.
\(p_0\), \(p_i\) for \(i\in I\), and \(p_j\) for \(j\in J\) are real multivariate polynomials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y)\in X\times(Y\cap\mathbb Z^q)\) is optimized subject to polynomial equalities and inequalities.

notation.meaning: finite inequality and equality index sets

children.title: Mixed-Integer Fractional Optimization

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Fractional Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer optimization whose objective or constraints contain one ratio or a finite sum of well-defined ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=X\times(Y\cap\mathbb Z^q)\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), and \(q\geq1\). A mixed-integer fractional optimization problem is an optimization problem over \(D\) whose objective or at least one constraint contains an expression
\[
R(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{f_k(x,y)}{g_k(x,y)},
\]
where \(K\in\mathbb N\), each \(f_k,g_k:D\to\mathbb R\), and \(g_k(x,y)\neq0\) for every \((x,y)\in D\). Under the common sign convention \(g_k(x,y)>0\) on \(D\), every ratio is well-defined without denominator sign changes. The case \(K=1\) is a single-ratio model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer fractional problem contains one ratio or a finite sum of ratios, with every denominator nonzero throughout the modeled domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D=X\times(Y\cap\mathbb Z^q)\), with \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q\), and \(q\geq1\).
\(K\in\mathbb N\) and \(f_k,g_k:D\to\mathbb R\) for \(k=1,\ldots,K\).
\(g_k(x,y)\neq0\) for all \((x,y)\in D\) and \(k=1,\ldots,K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^K f_k(x,y)/g_k(x,y)\) is well-defined for every \((x,y)\in D\).

children.title: Mixed-Integer Signomial Optimization
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models with signomial or generalized geometric structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Signomial Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer optimization containing signomial expressions in positive continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), let \(y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\), and let \(K\in\mathbb N\). For coefficient functions \(c_k:Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\to\mathbb R\) and exponents \(\alpha_{ik}\in\mathbb R\), an integer-parameterized signomial expression is
\[
s(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k(y)\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_{ik}}.
\]
For every fixed admissible integer assignment \(y\), the map \(x\mapsto s(x,y)\) is a signomial. A mixed-integer signomial optimization problem uses at least one such expression in its objective or constraints. Unlike a posynomial, a signomial may have negative coefficients; these signed terms generally prevent the standard log transformation from producing a convex posynomial model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer signomial model uses finite sums of real-power monomials in positive continuous variables, permits signed coefficients, and includes integer decisions.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\), and \(q\geq1\).
\(K\in\mathbb N\), \(\alpha_{ik}\in\mathbb R\), and \(c_k:Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(x,y)=\sum_{k=1}^K c_k(y)\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_{ik}}\) is a signomial in \(x\) for every fixed \(y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\).

notation.meaning: real exponent of continuous variable i in term k
possibly signed coefficient for integer assignment y

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the model class, its signomial expressions and positive-domain requirements, and an epigraph representation of a signomial objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-integer signomial program has continuous and/or discrete variables \(x\) and the form \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=a\), \(Bx\le b\), \(g(x)\le0\), and \(q(x)+\sigma(x)\le0\), where \(f\), \(g\), and \(q\) are convex in their stated roles and \(\sigma(x)=\sum_{j=1}^J c_j\prod_{i=1}^N x_i^{p_{ji}}\) with real coefficients and exponents. Every variable occurring in a signomial term is assigned a strictly positive lower bound. A signomial objective \(s(x)\) can be replaced, while retaining the remaining constraints, by the objective \(\min\mu\) and constraint \(s(x)-\mu\le0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer signomial program combines continuous or discrete variables, linear constraints, convex nonlinear constraints, and generalized signomial constraints. A signomial is a sum of real-coefficient products of real powers. Variables occurring in signomial terms are restricted to strictly positive lower bounds. A signomial objective can be represented epigraphically by minimizing an auxiliary variable while retaining the original feasible-set constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Complementarity Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed-integer nonlinear models containing componentwise complementarity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A mixed-integer complementarity model contains continuous variables \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), integer variables \(y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\), and at least one complementarity system
\[
0\leq u(x,y)\ \perp\ v(x,y)\geq0,
\]
meaning componentwise that \(u_i(x,y)\geq0\), \(v_i(x,y)\geq0\), and \(u_i(x,y)v_i(x,y)=0\) for every \(i\). Each component therefore enforces the disjunction \(u_i(x,y)=0\) or \(v_i(x,y)=0\), in addition to the explicit integrality restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model combines integer variables with nonnegative function pairs whose componentwise products must vanish.
assumptions_latex: \(u,v:X\times Y\to\mathbb R^r\).
\(y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_i(x,y)\geq0,\ v_i(x,y)\geq0,\ u_i(x,y)v_i(x,y)=0\) for all \(i\).

children.title: Continuous Nonconvex NLP Relaxation Interface
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex continuous relaxation obtained by dropping integrality.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Nonconvex NLP Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous relaxation formed by replacing integrality with a continuous containing set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the minimization problem
\[
v_{\mathrm{MI}}=\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\leq0,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\}.
\]
Its continuous nonconvex NLP relaxation replaces \(Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\) by a continuous set \(\widehat Y\supseteq Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\):
\[
v_{\mathrm{NLP}}=\inf\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\leq0,\ x\in X,\ y\in\widehat Y\}.
\]
The nonlinear functions are otherwise retained. Consequently, if both infima are well-defined, the relaxation satisfies \(v_{\mathrm{NLP}}\leq v_{\mathrm{MI}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dropping integrality enlarges the feasible set; a global relaxation solution gives a lower bound for minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\subseteq\widehat Y\subseteq\mathbb R^q\).
Both problems use the same objective and nonlinear constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{MI}}\subseteq F_{\mathrm{NLP}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{NLP}}\leq v_{\mathrm{MI}}\).

notation.meaning: continuous relaxation of the integer domain

children.title: Integer-Fixed Nonconvex NLP Interface
children.top_down_role: Continuous nonconvex subproblem associated with a fixed discrete assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Fixed Nonconvex NLP Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous nonconvex subproblem induced by a prescribed integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a mixed-integer minimization model with feasible integer domain \(Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\), choose \(\bar y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\) and substitute \(y=\bar y\). The integer-fixed NLP is
\[
v(\bar y)=\inf\{f(x,\bar y):g(x,\bar y)\leq0,\ x\in X\}.
\]
If this subproblem is feasible, every feasible \(x\) produces a feasible mixed-integer point \((x,\bar y)\). Its globally solved value satisfies \(v_{\mathrm{MI}}\leq v(\bar y)\); a merely local NLP solution supplies a feasible incumbent value but does not certify \(v(\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing the integers yields a continuous NLP; feasible solutions are incumbents, while only a global solve characterizes that fixed assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^q\).
The original problem is a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_{\mathrm{MI}}\leq v(\bar y)\) whenever the fixed NLP is feasible and solved globally.

notation.meaning: global value of the fixed-assignment NLP

children.title: Factorable Continuous Relaxation Interface
children.top_down_role: Transfer of expression structure and node domains to a factorable continuous solver.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorable Continuous Relaxation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structure-preserving transfer of a continuous relaxation to a factorable global NLP solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a continuous relaxation with variable box \(B\) and expressions represented by directed acyclic graphs whose leaves are variables or constants and whose internal nodes are supported unary or binary operations. Initialize each variable node with its interval from \(B\). Traverse every graph in topological order, transmit each operation and its child indices, and compute a valid interval enclosure for every node from its children. Pass the root expressions, constraint senses, objective sense, and node intervals to the continuous solver. If an operation lacks a supported enclosure or has an undefined interval domain, stop and report the interface failure; otherwise output the factorable relaxation instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transfer expression graphs and interval domains recursively; reject unsupported operations or nodes whose interval domains are undefined.
assumptions_latex: \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\) is a valid variable box.
Every transmitted operation has a valid interval extension on its child intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output preserves the relaxation's expression graph and supplies a valid interval enclosure at every node.

notation.meaning: box domain of the continuous relaxation

children.title: Local NLP Primal Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of local nonlinear optimization for incumbent generation and repair.

knowledge_statements.title: Local NLP Primal Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Incumbent generation by locally optimizing continuous variables after fixing an integer assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a MINLP \(\min\{f(x,y):g(x,y)\le 0,\ h(x,y)=0,\ x\in X,\ y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^p\}\), choose \(\bar y\in Y\cap\mathbb Z^p\) and a continuous starting point \(x^0\in X\). Apply a local NLP solver to \(\min_{x\in X} f(x,\bar y)\) subject to \(g(x,\bar y)\le0\) and \(h(x,\bar y)=0\). If the returned \(\hat x\) satisfies the original constraints within prescribed feasibility tolerances, output \((\hat x,\bar y)\) as an incumbent candidate; otherwise report failure for this fixing. The interface supplies no global-optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix the integer variables, locally optimize the continuous variables, and accept the result as an incumbent only when it satisfies the original MINLP constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(Y\subseteq\mathbb R^p\).
The local NLP solver accepts the integer-fixed nonlinear subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible returned point \((\hat x,\bar y)\) is a valid MINLP incumbent, but need not be globally optimal.

notation.meaning: Point returned by the local NLP solver.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is mathematically coherent and fits the local NLP primal-interface container, but no inspectable source is supplied for this integer-fixing incumbent heuristic and its acceptance semantics.

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Lifting

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact expression-graph lifting before relaxation of primitive relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)\) be represented by a finite acyclic expression graph whose internal nodes apply primitives \(\phi_v\). Introduce one variable \(z_v\) for every internal node and impose \(z_v=\phi_v(z_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})\), interpreting leaf values as components or constants of \(x\). Replace each occurrence of the root expression by its root variable. The lifted feasible set projects onto the original feasible set because every \(x\) uniquely determines all node values by graph evaluation, while every point satisfying all defining equalities reproduces the same expression values. Replacing these equalities by outer relaxations produces an extended relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introduce a variable for every expression-graph node and primitive defining equality. The exact lifted model projects to the original model; relaxing those equalities yields an extended relaxation.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Every primitive is defined at the values admitted by its parent nodes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact lifting and original formulation have the same projection onto the original variables.

notation.meaning: Auxiliary value assigned to expression node v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation matches auxiliary-variable lifting and is internally precise, but the exact projection claim and extended-relaxation construction have no cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Common-Subexpression Management
children.top_down_role: Shared and duplicated expression structures affecting relaxation consistency.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Subexpression Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation strength depends on whether repeated expressions share one lifted variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the same expression \(q(x)\) occurs at two positions. A shared lifting introduces one variable \(z\) with \(z=q(x)\) and uses \(z\) at both positions. A duplicated lifting introduces \(z_1=q(x)\) and \(z_2=q(x)\). These exact formulations have the same projection. If each defining equality is independently replaced by an outer relaxation \((x,z_i)\in R\), the duplicated relaxation may admit \(z_1\ne z_2\); adding \(z_1=z_2\), or using the shared variable, removes this inconsistency and yields a relaxation contained in the independently duplicated one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact shared and duplicated liftings are equivalent, but independently relaxing duplicates can permit inconsistent values. Sharing the auxiliary variable or equating duplicates cannot weaken the relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Both occurrences represent the identical function \(q\) on the same variable domain.
\(R\) is an outer relaxation of \(\{(x,z):z=q(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The shared relaxation is contained in the independently duplicated relaxation, with equality after imposing \(z_1=z_2\).

notation.meaning: Outer relaxation of the subexpression graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits common-subexpression management and the containment claim is plausible, but no source supports the distinction between shared and independently relaxed duplicate liftings.

children.title: Integer-Aware Expression Reformulation

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Aware Expression Reformulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear formulation for a binary variable multiplied by a bounded continuous expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(L\le x\le U\), and introduce \(z=bx\). The product graph over this mixed domain has the exact linear convex-hull representation \[Lb\le z\le Ub,\qquad x-U(1-b)\le z\le x-L(1-b).\] For \(b=0\), these inequalities force \(z=0\); for \(b=1\), they force \(z=x\). Relaxing \(b\) to \([0,1]\) gives the convex hull of \(\{(b,x,z):b\in\{0,1\},\ L\le x\le U,\ z=bx\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary–bounded-continuous product has an exact four-inequality linear formulation; relaxing the binary variable produces the product graph’s convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(L,U\in\mathbb R\) with \(L\le U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four inequalities are exact for binary \(b\), and with \(0\le b\le1\) describe the convex hull.

notation.meaning: Bounded continuous variable or expression value.
Auxiliary variable representing the product bx.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four inequalities and convex-hull claim are standard and correctly stated for a binary variable times a bounded continuous variable, and the representation fits the container; however, no source or locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Primitive Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull relaxation of a univariate convex primitive over a compact interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Reversal Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign reversal exchanges convex and concave primitive estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) on a convex set \(D\), \(f\) is convex on \(D\) if and only if \(-f\) is concave on \(D\). If \(\underline f\le f\le\overline f\) on \(D\), then \(-\overline f\le -f\le-\underline f\). Consequently, a convex underestimator and concave overestimator for \(f\) become, after negation, respectively a concave overestimator and convex underestimator for \(-f\). For a lifted equality \(z=f(x)\), the substitution \(w=-z\) transfers the relaxation to \(w=-f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating a primitive reverses curvature and swaps lower and upper estimators, with the lifted output variable also negated.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is convex.
All estimators are finite on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Negation maps valid estimator pairs for \(f\) to valid curvature-reversed estimator pairs for \(-f\).

notation.meaning: Lower and upper estimators of f.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Curvature Primitive Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise graph relaxation for a primitive whose curvature changes across its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a continuous primitive \(f:[\ell,u]\to\mathbb R\), select a partition \(\ell=t_0<\cdots<t_m=u\) such that a valid convex underestimator \(f_i^{\mathrm{cv}}\) and concave overestimator \(f_i^{\mathrm{cc}}\) are available on every \(I_i=[t_{i-1},t_i]\). Form \(R_i=\{(x,z):x\in I_i,\ f_i^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le z\le f_i^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\}\). Retain the union \(\bigcup_iR_i\) through a disjunctive model, or use its convex hull as a node relaxation. Output the resulting outer approximation; refine the partition when tighter bounds are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition a mixed-curvature domain, construct valid lower and upper estimators on each piece, and model their union or convex hull as an outer relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous on \([\ell,u]\).
Each estimator pair is valid throughout its assigned subinterval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed union, and therefore its convex hull, contains \(\{(x,f(x)):x\in[\ell,u]\}\).

notation.meaning: Convex lower and concave upper estimators on subinterval i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The partition-and-estimator procedure is a suitable algorithm for the mixed-curvature primitive-graph container and its outer-approximation conclusion is precise, but it lacks a cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Singular Domain-Safeguard Regimes
children.top_down_role: Primitive graphs whose relaxations depend on explicit domain safeguards.

children.title: Domain-Restricted Primitives
children.top_down_role: Primitive graphs requiring explicit admissible-domain control.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Restricted Primitives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility condition for evaluating and relaxing a primitive on a node domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a primitive \(f\) have effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)\in\mathbb R\}\), and let \(I=[\ell,u]\) be the interval supplied by bound propagation. A finite-valued primitive relaxation on the entire node interval is admissible only if \(I\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(I\not\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\), domain propagation must replace it by \(I\cap\operatorname{dom}f\); an empty intersection certifies infeasibility. When the domain is open at an endpoint, inclusion requires a strict bound or a separate limit-safe representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite primitive relaxation requires the propagated interval to lie inside the primitive’s domain; otherwise intersect with the domain, reject emptiness, and safeguard open boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \(I=[\ell,u]\) is the current interval enclosure of the primitive argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whole-interval evaluation is admissible exactly when \(I\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\); otherwise domain contraction or a safeguarded representation is required.

notation.meaning: Effective real-valued domain of the primitive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits domain-restricted primitives, but its claims about mandatory domain propagation, strict endpoint bounds, and limit-safe alternatives require an authoritative source and precise locator.

children.title: Singular Primitive Behavior
children.top_down_role: Primitive graphs exhibiting poles, blow-up, or undefined boundary behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Primitive Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite relaxations when an interval reaches a logarithmic singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=\log x\), whose real domain is \((0,\infty)\). On every interval \([\ell,u]\) with \(0<\ell<u\), \(f\) is finite and concave and admits finite graph bounds. If the lower endpoint is relaxed to \(\ell=0\), then \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\); the graph over \((0,u]\) is unbounded below, and evaluation at zero is undefined. Hence no finite-valued relaxation that claims validity at \(x=0\) can represent this primitive graph without an explicit domain exclusion or extended-value convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithm becomes unbounded below and undefined as its argument approaches zero, so a relaxation touching zero needs explicit domain exclusion or extended values.
assumptions_latex: The formulation uses ordinary real-valued, rather than extended-real, primitive values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Allowing \(x=0\) destroys any finite whole-interval graph relaxation for \(\log x\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The logarithmic singularity is correctly characterized and failure_boundary is the appropriate content kind, but no cited source supports the graph-relaxation consequence.

children.title: Boundary-Safe Relaxation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relaxation regimes that remain valid near restricted or singular boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary-Safe Relaxation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient conditions for finite, valid primitive estimators near a domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be finite on an interval \(I=[\ell,u]\) contained in its effective domain. A boundary-safe relaxation regime consists of finite functions \(f^{\mathrm{cv}},f^{\mathrm{cc}}:I\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(f^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\le f(x)\le f^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\) for every \(x\in I\), with every formula and derivative used to construct them defined on \(I\). If a singular boundary \(a\notin\operatorname{dom}f\) is approached, safety requires a certified separation \(\ell\ge a+\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\), or a limit-valid extended-value formulation that never evaluates \(f\) at \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary safety requires valid finite estimators and defined construction formulas throughout the interval, plus positive separation from excluded singular boundaries unless extended values are modeled.
assumptions_latex: \(I=[\ell,u]\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\).
The relaxation is intended to use finite real-valued inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: These conditions make the estimator inequalities well-defined and valid over the entire node interval.

notation.meaning: Convex lower and concave upper estimators.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is locally appropriate and internally consistent, but the asserted boundary-safety regime, especially the positive-separation or extended-value alternative, has no inspectable supporting citation.

children.title: Bilinear McCormick Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Box-domain convexification families for bilinear graph relations.

children.title: Continuous Bilinear Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Relaxations for products of bounded continuous variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Bilinear Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick convex-hull relaxation for a product of two bounded continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(w=xy\), where both intervals are nonempty and bounded. The convex hull of the bilinear graph over the rectangle is described by \[w\ge \ell_xy+\ell_yx-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y,\] \[w\le u_xy+\ell_yx-u_x\ell_y,\qquad w\le \ell_xy+u_yx-\ell_xu_y.\] These four McCormick inequalities therefore give the tightest convex relaxation of the isolated bounded bilinear graph in the original \((x,y,w)\)-space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four McCormick inequalities describe the convex hull of a bounded continuous bilinear product graph.
assumptions_latex: \(-\infty<\ell_x\le u_x<\infty\) and \(-\infty<\ell_y\le u_y<\infty\).
\(x\) and \(y\) are continuous variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four displayed inequalities describe \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,w):w=xy\}\) over the bounding rectangle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The four McCormick inequalities and isolated-graph convex-hull conclusion are mathematically standard, precise, and correctly classified as a representation, but no source with a section, theorem, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Binary–Continuous Product Convexification
children.top_down_role: Convexification specialized to products with a binary factor.

assumptions_latex: \(L\le x\le U\), where \(L,U\in\mathbb R\) and \(L\le U\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{(b,x,w):b\in\{0,1\},\ L\le x\le U,\ w=bx\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear convex hull for one binary and one bounded continuous factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(x\in[L,U]\), and \(w=bx\), the convex hull in \((b,x,w)\)-space is described exactly by
\[
0\le b\le1,\qquad Lb\le w\le Ub,
\]
\[
x-U(1-b)\le w\le x-L(1-b),\qquad L\le x\le U.
\]
Thus replacing the product equality by these four product inequalities and relaxing \(b\) to \([0,1]\) introduces no convex-hull gap for the isolated product graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four linear inequalities give the exact convex hull of a product between a binary variable and a bounded continuous variable.
knowledge_statements.title: Binary–Continuous Product Convexification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact binary–continuous product hull is mathematically standard and correctly stated, and representation is an appropriate knowledge kind. No inspectable citation is supplied for the hull claim.

children.title: Partitioned Bilinear Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Piecewise convexification over subdivided variable domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Partitioned Bilinear Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Union of cellwise McCormick hulls over a finite partition, typically represented by a mixed-integer disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G_k=\{(x,y,w):x\in[t_{k-1},t_k],\ y\in[L_y,U_y],\ w=xy\}\), and define
\[
R_{\mathcal P}=\bigcup_{k=1}^K\operatorname{conv}(G_k),
\]
where each \(\operatorname{conv}(G_k)\) is described by the four McCormick inequalities on its cell. If \(G=\{(x,y,w):x\in[L_x,U_x],\ y\in[L_y,U_y],\ w=xy\}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{Mc}}=\operatorname{conv}(G)\), then
\[
G\subseteq R_{\mathcal P}\subseteq R_{\mathrm{Mc}}.
\]
If \(\mathcal P'\) refines \(\mathcal P\), then \(R_{\mathcal P'}\subseteq R_{\mathcal P}\). Thus the disjunctive, generally nonconvex partitioned relaxation cannot become weaker under refinement; it can be modeled using cell-selection variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The union of cellwise McCormick hulls is a valid bilinear relaxation contained in the full-box McCormick hull, and refining the partition cannot enlarge it.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in[L_x,U_x]\) and \(y\in[L_y,U_y]\)
\(L_x=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_K=U_x\) is a finite partition
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\subseteq R_{\mathcal P}\subseteq R_{\mathrm{Mc}}\), and \(R_{\mathcal P'}\subseteq R_{\mathcal P}\) whenever \(\mathcal P'\) refines \(\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: graph of the bilinear product over the full box
union of the cellwise McCormick hulls

children.title: Multilinear Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Convexification families for products of three or more factors.

children.title: Recursive McCormick Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Recursive bilinear decompositions and grouping families.

assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in[L_i,U_i]\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\)
A full binary parenthesization of \(\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\) is fixed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,w):w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\}\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(R_T)\).

notation.meaning: auxiliary variable associated with tree node v

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive relaxation associated with a fixed binary grouping tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Create a leaf variable \(z_i=x_i\) for every factor. For each internal node \(v\) with children \(p,q\), introduce \(z_v\), compute valid bounds on \(z_p,z_q\), and impose the four McCormick inequalities relaxing \(z_v=z_pz_q\). At the root \(r\), set \(w=z_r\). The resulting set \(R_T\) is convex and satisfies
\[
\{(x,z,w):z_v=\prod_{i\text{ below }v}x_i,\ w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\}\subseteq R_T.
\]
Different parenthesizations can produce different relaxations, so the grouping tree is part of the algorithmic specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursively replace a multilinear term by bilinear products and apply McCormick inequalities at every internal node; the chosen grouping can affect relaxation strength.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive McCormick Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recursive construction, validity statement, and dependence on the grouping tree are coherent, and algorithm is the correct knowledge kind. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Direct Multilinear Hull Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Extended convexifications treating multilinear terms as unified objects.

assumptions_latex: \(x_i\in[L_i,U_i]\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\)
\(V=\prod_{i=1}^n\{L_i,U_i\}\) is the box-vertex set
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(G)=\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(H)\).

notation.meaning: multilinear product graph over the box

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact vertex extended formulation for one multilinear monomial on a box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
G=\{(x,w):x\in\textstyle\prod_{i=1}^n[L_i,U_i],\ w=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i\},
\]
introduce weights \(\lambda_v\ge0\) for \(v\in V\) and define
\[
H=\left\{(x,w,\lambda):\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v=1,\ x=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_vv,\ w=\sum_{v\in V}\lambda_v\prod_{i=1}^n v_i\right\}.
\]
Because a multilinear function is obtained by multilinear interpolation of its vertex values, \(\operatorname{conv}(G)=\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(H)\). The formulation is exact but has \(2^n\) vertex weights before exploiting structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilinear product's box graph has an exact extended convex-hull formulation using convex weights on all box vertices.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Multilinear Hull Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vertex-weight formulation correctly expresses the convex hull of a multilinear graph over a box, and representation fits the container. The exact-hull claim lacks an inspectable citation.

children.title: Disaggregated Multilinear Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Disaggregated formulations exploiting discrete or partition structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Disaggregated Multilinear Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disaggregated convex-hull formulation over a finite box partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V_k\) be the vertices of \(D_k\). Introduce \(\lambda_{kv}\ge0\) and \(\delta_k\ge0\), and impose
\[
\sum_{k=1}^K\delta_k=1,\qquad \sum_{v\in V_k}\lambda_{kv}=\delta_k\quad(k=1,\ldots,K),
\]
\[
x=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{v\in V_k}\lambda_{kv}v,\qquad
w=\sum_{k=1}^K\sum_{v\in V_k}\lambda_{kv}\prod_i v_i.
\]
The resulting set \(H_D\) projects to \(\operatorname{conv}(\bigcup_{k=1}^K G_k)\). If \(\delta\) is required to be one-hot, the formulation selects one cellwise hull \(\operatorname{conv}(G_k)\), yielding a mixed-integer relaxation of the partitioned multilinear graph; the vertex-weight constraints alone do not enforce the nonlinear graph within the selected cell.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cell-specific vertex weights describe the convex hull of the union of the cell graphs; one-hot cell selectors select a cellwise hull and therefore give a mixed-integer relaxation, not the exact nonlinear graph.
assumptions_latex: \(D=\bigcup_{k=1}^K D_k\) is a finite partition into boxes
\(G_k=\{(x,w):x\in D_k,\ w=\prod_i x_i\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}(H_D)=\operatorname{conv}(G)\), where \(G=\bigcup_{k=1}^K G_k\).

notation.meaning: multilinear graph restricted to partition cell k

children.title: Ratio-Reciprocal Relaxation Family
children.top_down_role: Domain-sensitive relaxations for reciprocal and ratio structure.

children.title: Direct Ratio Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Direct convexification of bounded numerator–denominator relations.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in[L_x,U_x]\) and \(y\in[L_y,U_y]\)
\(0<L_y\le U_y\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w=x/y\) is equivalently represented by \(x=wy\), with \(w\) bounded before convexification.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-sign ratio reformulated as one bilinear equality before convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define valid ratio bounds by
\[
L_w=\min\{L_x/L_y,L_x/U_y,U_x/L_y,U_x/U_y\},\qquad
U_w=\max\{L_x/L_y,L_x/U_y,U_x/L_y,U_x/U_y\}.
\]
Since \(y>0\), the relation \(w=x/y\) is equivalent to \(x=wy\) with \(w\in[L_w,U_w]\). A direct convex relaxation is therefore obtained by applying the four McCormick inequalities to the product \(wy\) and identifying its product variable with \(x\). It is valid on the stated box, although it need not equal the convex hull of the ratio graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a positive bounded denominator, a ratio becomes a bounded bilinear equality; McCormick inequalities then provide a direct valid convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Ratio Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-denominator reformulation, corner-derived ratio bounds, and McCormick relaxation are valid and appropriately classified as a representation. The variant requires a specific supporting citation.

children.title: Lifted Reciprocal Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Lifted separation of reciprocal and product structure.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in[L_x,U_x]\) and \(y\in[L_y,U_y]\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w=x/y\) is lifted as \(t=1/y\) and \(w=xt\), each replaced by a valid convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifted ratio relaxation using reciprocal envelopes and a bilinear product relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Introduce \(t\in[1/U_y,1/L_y]\) and replace \(t=1/y\) by the convex-hull inequalities
\[
t\ge 1/y,
\qquad
t\le \frac{L_y+U_y-y}{L_yU_y}.
\]
Equivalently, the first constraint may be written as the convex condition \(yt\ge1\) with \(y,t>0\). Introduce \(w\) and relax \(w=xt\) by the four McCormick inequalities over \([L_x,U_x]\times[1/U_y,1/L_y]\). Every point satisfying \(w=x/y\) admits \(t=1/y\) and is feasible in this lifted convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate a ratio into a reciprocal and a product, convexify the reciprocal graph, and apply McCormick inequalities to the lifted product.
knowledge_statements.title: Lifted Reciprocal Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal graph inequalities and lifted McCormick construction are mathematically coherent, with positivity making the reciprocal epigraph convex. No inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Quadratic Lower-Bounding Families
children.top_down_role: Lower-bounding systems specialized to indefinite quadratic structure.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Global Optimization: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Global Optimization: Theory, Algorithms, and Applications

children.title: AlphaBB Diagonal Convexification Family
children.top_down_role: Curvature-correction families based on diagonal or spectral information.

children.title: AlphaBB Curvature Correction
children.top_down_role: AlphaBB lower-bounding structures based on curvature compensation.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on the box \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[l_i,u_i]\)
\(\alpha_i\ge0\) for every \(i\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_\alpha(x)=f(x)+\sum_i\alpha_i(l_i-x_i)(u_i-x_i)\) is a convex underestimator whenever \(\nabla^2f(x)+2\operatorname{Diag}(\alpha)\succeq0\) on \(B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boxwise AlphaBB underestimator with a diagonal separable correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
f_\alpha(x)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i(l_i-x_i)(u_i-x_i).
\]
For every \(x\in B\), each factor satisfies \((l_i-x_i)(u_i-x_i)\le0\), so \(f_\alpha(x)\le f(x)\), with equality at every vertex of \(B\). Moreover,
\[
\nabla^2 f_\alpha(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)+2\operatorname{Diag}(\alpha).
\]
Consequently, if \(\nabla^2 f(x)+2\operatorname{Diag}(\alpha)\succeq0\) for all \(x\in B\), then \(f_\alpha\) is a convex underestimator of \(f\) throughout \(B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: AlphaBB adds a nonpositive separable quadratic term that preserves underestimation and shifts the Hessian diagonally until the result is convex.
knowledge_statements.title: AlphaBB Curvature Correction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The AlphaBB correction has the correct sign, Hessian shift, underestimation property, and convexity condition. Property fits the terminal container, but the nontrivial AlphaBB statement lacks a citation.

children.title: Diagonal Convexification
children.top_down_role: Convexification through diagonal curvature modifications.

assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2(B)\), where \(B=\prod_i[l_i,u_i]\)
\(D=\operatorname{Diag}(d)\) with \(d_i\ge0\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_D\) is convex on \(B\) exactly when \(\nabla^2f(x)+2D\succeq0\) for every \(x\in B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient Hessian condition for a fixed diagonal correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(d_i\ge0\), define
\[
g_D(x)=f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^n d_i(l_i-x_i)(u_i-x_i).
\]
Then \(g_D(x)\le f(x)\) on \(B\), and
\[
\nabla^2g_D(x)=\nabla^2f(x)+2D.
\]
Because \(B\) is convex and \(g_D\) is twice continuously differentiable, the complete convexification condition is
\[
\nabla^2f(x)+2D\succeq0\qquad\text{for every }x\in B.
\]
Thus choosing a diagonal correction amounts to finding a componentwise nonnegative \(d\) satisfying this semi-infinite positive-semidefiniteness condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonnegative diagonal correction convexifies a twice differentiable function exactly when the corrected Hessian is positive semidefinite throughout the box.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Convexification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a twice continuously differentiable function on a convex box, the stated positive-semidefinite Hessian condition is necessary and sufficient for the fixed diagonal correction to be convex. Condition is the correct knowledge kind, but a source is missing.

children.title: Spectral Parameter Selection
children.top_down_role: Spectral information used to calibrate curvature corrections.

assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2(B)\) on a box \(B\)
\(\underline\lambda\le\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\) for every \(x\in B\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha=\max\{0,-\underline\lambda/2\}\) makes \(\nabla^2f(x)+2\alpha I\succeq0\) on \(B\).

notation.meaning: uniform lower bound on the least Hessian eigenvalue

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform spectral rule based on a certified lower Hessian-eigenvalue bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a certified scalar \(\underline\lambda\) satisfies
\[
\underline\lambda\le\inf_{x\in B}\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x)).
\]
Choose the common diagonal parameter
\[
\alpha=\max\{0,-\underline\lambda/2\}.
\]
Then, for every \(x\in B\),
\[
\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x)+2\alpha I)=\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))+2\alpha\ge0.
\]
Hence this spectral choice guarantees convexity of the AlphaBB underestimator. A more negative lower eigenvalue bound remains valid but produces a larger correction and generally a weaker lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half the magnitude of a certified negative lower Hessian-eigenvalue bound gives a uniform diagonal shift that guarantees convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Parameter Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform spectral shift follows correctly from the certified lower bound on the minimum Hessian eigenvalue, and condition fits the parameter-selection leaf. A specific source is required.

children.title: RLT-Based Quadratic Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Lifted linear relaxations generated from products of bounds and constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies finite linear inequalities \(a_r^\top x-b_r\ge0\) and bounds \(l_i\le x_i\le u_i\)
\(X\in\mathbb S^n\) replaces \(xx^\top\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every original feasible point lifts to \((x,X)=(x,xx^\top)\) satisfying all generated RLT constraints.

notation.meaning: linearization operator replacing each product x_i x_j by X_ij

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-level RLT generated from products of valid linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select pairs of valid nonnegative affine factors \(p(x)\ge0\) and \(q(x)\ge0\), including bound factors such as \(x_i-l_i\) and \(u_i-x_i\). Form \(p(x)q(x)\ge0\), expand it, and apply \(\mathcal L(x_ix_j)=X_{ij}\) to obtain a linear inequality in \((x,X)\). Apply the same substitution to every quadratic objective and constraint, impose \(X_{ij}=X_{ji}\), and solve the resulting linear relaxation. Since \(p(x)q(x)\ge0\) holds at every feasible \(x\), its lift \((x,xx^\top)\) satisfies every RLT inequality, so the construction gives a valid lower-bounding relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: RLT multiplies valid nonnegative affine constraints, expands the products, and replaces each quadratic monomial by a matrix variable to obtain valid linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: RLT-Based Quadratic Relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The first-level RLT generation procedure and validity argument are correctly scoped, and algorithm is an appropriate knowledge kind. The construction has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Semidefinite Quadratic Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Matrix-lifting relaxations for quadratic interactions.

assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) replaces \(xx^\top\)
Quadratic expressions are written as \(x^\top Qx+2q^\top x+c\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\) yields a convex relaxation containing every rank-one lift.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order Shor matrix lifting for quadratically constrained optimization.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Semidefinite Relaxations p. 75
source_refs.source_title: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Replace every quadratic form \(x^\top Qx\) by \(\langle Q,X\rangle\) and impose
\[
Y=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&X\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
By the Schur complement, this is equivalent to \(X-xx^\top\succeq0\). Every original point has the rank-one lift \(X=xx^\top\), so linearized quadratic constraints together with \(Y\succeq0\) define a convex outer relaxation. Dropping the nonconvex condition \(\operatorname{rank}(Y)=1\) creates the relaxation; a feasible rank-one optimal solution recovers a globally feasible solution of equal relaxation value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lift quadratic products into a matrix, require the homogeneous lift to be positive semidefinite, and omit its nonconvex rank-one condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Quadratic Relaxations

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2 Semidefinite Relaxations p. 75
source_witnesses.source_title: Moments, Positive Polynomials and Their Applications

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordering of Quadratic and Conic Relaxation Values
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison chain among lower and upper quadratic values and parameterized conic-relaxation values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \psi_*\leq\phi_*\leq\psi\!\left(1-\frac{2}{\pi}\right)\leq\psi\!\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right)\leq\phi^*\leq\psi^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower conic bound, lower quadratic value, two parameterized relaxation values, upper quadratic value, and upper conic bound occur in the displayed nondecreasing order.

children.title: Second-Order Cone Quadratic Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Conic relaxations exploiting convexifiable quadratic substructure.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Cone Quadratic Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: SOC representation of a convex quadratic term obtained within a nonconvex MINLP relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) and choose \(R\) with \(Q=R^{\mathsf T}R\). The convex quadratic epigraph constraint \(t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2q^{\mathsf T}x+c\) is equivalent, after setting \(s=t-2q^{\mathsf T}x-c\), to the second-order-cone system \[\left\|(2Rx,\,s-1)\right\|_2\le s+1.\] Consequently, replacing each convexifiable quadratic component by this system, while relaxing the remaining nonconvex products with valid lifted constraints, gives a conic outer relaxation of the original feasible set and hence a valid lower-bounding problem for minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph has an exact second-order-cone representation; combining these representations with valid relaxations of remaining products yields a global lower-bounding conic model.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb S^n_+\).
\(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(q\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(c,t\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(t\ge x^{\mathsf T}Qx+2q^{\mathsf T}x+c\iff \|(2Rx,s-1)\|_2\le s+1\), where \(s=t-2q^{\mathsf T}x-c\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard SOC reformulation of a positive-semidefinite quadratic epigraph

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The SOC reformulation and lower-bounding interpretation are mathematically standard and consistent, but no inspectable citation is supplied for the exact representation and relaxation claim.

children.title: Bound-Factor RLT
