children.title: Global Root Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds valid over the complete mixed-integer domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Root Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A root-node bound valid over the complete feasible set of a minimization MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the minimization problem \(v^*:=\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in F\}\), where \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^p\). A finite scalar \(L_0\) is a certified global root lower bound if its derivation establishes \(L_0\le f(x,y)\) for every \((x,y)\in F\). Equivalently, \(L_0\le v^*\). In particular, if a root relaxation has feasible region \(R_0\supseteq F\) and objective underestimator \(\underline f_0\) satisfying \(\underline f_0(x,y)\le f(x,y)\) on \(F\), then any certified value \(L_0\le\inf_{(x,y)\in R_0}\underline f_0(x,y)\) is valid globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A root lower bound is certified when it does not exceed the objective of any feasible mixed-integer point, commonly through a globally valid relaxation and underestimator.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^p\) is the complete feasible set.
The problem is interpreted as minimization.

notation.meaning: Global infimum of the objective over F

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 Lower Bounds p. 128

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 Lower Bounds p. 128

children.title: Node-Local Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower bounds valid over individual discrete or spatial subregions.

knowledge_statements.title: Node-Local Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A lower bound whose validity is restricted to one branch-and-bound or spatial subregion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^p\) be the domain represented by search node \(k\), and set \(F_k:=F\cap D_k\). A scalar \(L_k\) is a certified node-local lower bound when \(L_k\le f(x,y)\) for every \((x,y)\in F_k\), equivalently \(L_k\le\inf_{(x,y)\in F_k}f(x,y)\), with the convention \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). The certificate is transferable to a descendant \(j\) whenever \(D_j\subseteq D_k\), but it need not bound feasible points outside \(D_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-local lower bound applies only within its node’s subdomain. It remains valid for descendants but generally not for unrelated regions.
assumptions_latex: \(F_k=F\cap D_k\) is the node-feasible set.
The problem is interpreted as minimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_k\le\inf_{(x,y)\in F_k}f(x,y)\).

notation.meaning: Discrete or spatial domain assigned to node k
Feasible set restricted to node k

source_refs.locator: 3.4.2 Lower Bounds p. 128

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4.2 Lower Bounds p. 128

children.title: Integer-Feasible Upper Bounds
children.top_down_role: Upper bounds supplied by verified mixed-integer feasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Feasible Upper Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An incumbent objective value certified by mixed-integer and nonlinear feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v^*:=\inf\{f(x,y):(x,y)\in F\}\), let \((\hat x,\hat y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^p\) satisfy every defining constraint of \(F\). Then \(U:=f(\hat x,\hat y)\) is a certified upper bound: \(v^*\le U\). If feasibility or objective evaluation is numerical, the certificate must use validated enclosures sufficient to establish membership in \(F\) and an outward-rounded value \(\overline f(\hat x,\hat y)\ge f(\hat x,\hat y)\); then \(U:=\overline f(\hat x,\hat y)\) is the certified bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any verified feasible mixed-integer point supplies an upper bound for minimization; validated numerical checks must round the reported objective upward.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb Z^p\) is the complete feasible set.
The objective is minimized.

children.title: Bound Provenance
children.top_down_role: Traceability of reported bounds to relaxations, domains, and search nodes.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound Provenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal audit data identifying the domain, derivation, and numerical validity of a reported bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound-provenance record may be represented by \(P=(s,k,D,m,a,\tau,\rho)\), where \(s\in\{\mathrm{lower},\mathrm{upper}\}\) is the bound sense, \(k\) identifies the root or search node, \(D\) is its validity domain, \(m\) identifies the relaxation, feasible point, or inference producing the bound, \(a\) records assumptions and tolerances, \(\tau\) is the solver termination status, and \(\rho\) is a replayable witness or audit reference. A reported scalar \(b\) is provenance-complete only when these fields determine the precise quantified claim—either \(b\le f(z)\) on \(F\cap D\) or \(b\ge v^*\) via a certified feasible point—and permit its validity conditions to be checked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound provenance records what the bound means, where it applies, how it was produced, its assumptions, termination status, and an auditable witness.
assumptions_latex: The underlying optimization problem and objective sense are fixed.
Every search-node identifier determines a unique validity domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) determines an auditable domain-qualified bound claim for \(b\).

notation.meaning: Domain on which the bound claim is valid

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed provenance tuple is a plausible representation, but its asserted completeness and required fields are normative and have no cited authoritative source.

children.title: Solver Status Semantics

knowledge_statements.title: Solver Status Semantics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical interpretation of solver termination labels through explicit certified predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed problem instance, define a status semantics as a map \(\Sigma:S\to\mathcal P(\mathcal C)\), where \(S\) is the set of solver status labels and \(\mathcal C\) is the set of mathematical claims about feasibility, bounds, gaps, and search completeness. A returned status \(s\in S\) certifies only the claims in \(\Sigma(s)\) whose documented preconditions and numerical-validity requirements are satisfied. Thus labels such as \(\mathrm{optimal}\), \(\mathrm{infeasible}\), \(\mathrm{time\_limit}\), or \(\mathrm{unknown}\) have no solver-independent certificate strength beyond the explicit predicates assigned by \(\Sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver status has mathematical meaning only through documented predicates specifying which feasibility, bound, gap, or completeness claims it certifies under stated conditions.
assumptions_latex: Solver labels and their documented preconditions are fixed for the implementation.
Certificate claims are expressed as mathematical predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) supports exactly the applicable claims selected by \(\Sigma(s)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The abstraction is coherent and the definition kind fits, but solver-status meanings are implementation-specific and no documentation or standard is cited for the asserted semantics.

children.title: Status-Dependent Certificate Reliability
children.top_down_role: Certificate strength under differing solver-status outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Status-Dependent Certificate Reliability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness condition coupling a solver status to its evidence and documented preconditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be the returned evidence, \(s\in S\) the termination status, and \(C\) a claimed mathematical certificate. The report \((s,E,C)\) is reliable precisely when a checker establishes \(\operatorname{Pre}(s,E)\), verifies \(\operatorname{Check}(E)=\mathrm{accept}\), and the documented soundness implication \[\operatorname{Pre}(s,E)\land\bigl(\operatorname{Check}(E)=\mathrm{accept}\bigr)\Longrightarrow C\] applies to the problem data actually solved. A status reporting interruption, numerical failure, local optimality, or unknown termination cannot be upgraded to a global certificate unless its accompanying evidence independently satisfies this implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate is reliable only when the status preconditions hold and an accepted witness soundly implies the precise claim for the actual problem data.
assumptions_latex: The checker and status preconditions are documented.
The checked instance is identical to the reported optimization instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Pre}(s,E)\land\operatorname{Check}(E)=\mathrm{accept}\Longrightarrow C\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition has the correct local role, but the claimed necessary-and-sufficient reliability criterion depends on a documented certificate format, checker, and soundness theorem for which no source is supplied.

children.title: Global MINLP Optimality Certificate
children.top_down_role: Certificate organization connecting feasible incumbents, valid global bounds, and complete search coverage.

children.title: Incumbent Feasibility Certification
children.top_down_role: Certification of discrete and nonlinear feasibility for a reported incumbent.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Feasibility Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A checkable witness that a reported incumbent belongs to the original MINLP feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:=\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:g_i(x,y)\le 0\ (i\in I),\ h_j(x,y)=0\ (j\in J)\}\), where \(Y\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\). An incumbent \((\hat x,\hat y)\) is feasibility-certified for the original MINLP when \(\hat x\in X\), \(\hat y\in Y\), \(g_i(\hat x,\hat y)\le 0\) for every \(i\in I\), and \(h_j(\hat x,\hat y)=0\) for every \(j\in J\). When validated numerical evaluation is used, its enclosures must establish these exact predicates. A check performed only to nonzero feasibility tolerances certifies membership in the corresponding declared relaxed feasible set, not by itself membership in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incumbent is certified for the original MINLP only when its domains, integrality, inequalities, and equalities are established exactly. A tolerance-based check certifies only the explicitly declared relaxed feasible set.
assumptions_latex: All original constraints and variable domains are available to the checker.
Any relaxed numerical feasibility convention is explicitly declared and distinguished from exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\hat x,\hat y)\in F\).

notation.meaning: Original inequality and equality constraint functions

children.title: Global Lower-Bound Certification
children.top_down_role: Certification of bounds covering all unresolved search regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Lower-Bound Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregation of domain-qualified lower bounds over a certified cover of the complete feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the original feasible set, and let \(D_1,\ldots,D_m\) be finitely many search domains satisfying \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^m D_k\). For every \(k\), suppose \(L_k\in\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is certified to satisfy \(L_k\le f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\cap D_k\), with \(L_k=+\infty\) permitted only when \(F\cap D_k=\varnothing\) is certified. If \(L:=\min_{1\le k\le m}L_k\) is finite, then \(L\le f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\), so \(L\) is a certified global lower bound. Domains removed from the active search may participate in this cover only through records that certify the required domain-qualified lower-bound or infeasibility claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of certified domain bounds is a global lower bound when the associated domains cover the complete feasible set and every removed domain has a valid lower-bound or infeasibility record.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^m D_k\).
Each \(L_k\) is certified on \(F\cap D_k\).
The aggregate \(L=\min_{1\le k\le m}L_k\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L\le f(z)\) for every \(z\in F\).

notation.meaning: Search domain in the certified cover
Certified lower bound on domain k

children.title: Optimality-Gap Certification
children.top_down_role: Absolute and relative gap certification regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimality-Gap Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute and scale-normalized guarantees derived from certified lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem, let \(L\le v^*\le U\) be certified finite bounds. The absolute gap \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}:=U-L\) certifies that the incumbent objective is at most \(G_{\mathrm{abs}}\) above the global optimum. Given \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\ge0\), absolute-gap termination is valid when \(U-L\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}\). Given a declared scale \(s(U,L)>0\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\), the relative gap \(G_{\mathrm{rel}}:=(U-L)/s(U,L)\) is certified, and relative-gap termination is valid when \(G_{\mathrm{rel}}\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\). The scale convention must accompany the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified lower and upper bounds yield an absolute gap. A relative gap is meaningful only with a positive, explicitly recorded scaling convention.
assumptions_latex: \(L\le v^*\le U\) are certified finite bounds.
The relative-gap scale \(s(U,L)\) is declared and strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le U-v^*\le U-L\), with \((U-L)/s(U,L)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\) under relative-gap termination.

notation.meaning: Relative optimality gap under the declared scale

children.title: Search-Tree Coverage Certification
children.top_down_role: Coverage of discrete and spatial alternatives through resolution or valid fathoming.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Coverage Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite audit showing that branching and valid terminal resolution account for every original feasible alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_0\) be a root domain satisfying \(F\subseteq D_0\). A search-tree coverage certificate is a finite rooted tree in which every internal node \(k\) has children \(C(k)\) satisfying \(F\cap D_k\subseteq\bigcup_{j\in C(k)}(F\cap D_j)\). Every leaf \(\ell\) must carry a checkable record that validly resolves \(F\cap D_\ell\), such as certified infeasibility, certified bound-based fathoming under the declared incumbent, or complete certified resolution. These conditions certify \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal L}(F\cap D_\ell)\) and that every discrete or spatial alternative represented by the root is covered by a valid terminal record.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coverage is certified by a finite tree whose children cover each parent’s feasible region and whose every leaf has a valid, checkable terminal-resolution record.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq D_0\).
Every branching step records a valid child-cover inclusion.
Every leaf has a checkable and applicable terminal-resolution certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{\ell\in\mathcal L}(F\cap D_\ell)\), and every \(\ell\in\mathcal L\) is validly resolved.

notation.meaning: Domain associated with tree node k

children.title: Global MINLP Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificate families establishing absence of mixed-integer feasible solutions.

children.title: Relaxation Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Infeasibility inherited from globally valid relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A relaxation contradiction proving infeasibility of the original MINLP on a specified domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a search domain \(D\), let \(F_D:=F\cap D\) be the original feasible set and let \(R_D\) be a globally valid relaxation satisfying \(F_D\subseteq R_D\). A checkable certificate that \(R_D=\varnothing\) is a relaxation infeasibility certificate for \(D\). It certifies \(F_D=\varnothing\), so the corresponding node may be fathomed without excluding any feasible MINLP point. The certificate is unsound if the asserted relaxation omits a feasible point of \(F_D\), or if infeasibility is merely an unverified numerical solver status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a valid relaxation contains every feasible point in a node and is itself certified infeasible, then the original node is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(F_D\subseteq R_D\) is established globally on the node domain.
The emptiness of \(R_D\) has a checkable certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_D=\varnothing\Longrightarrow F_D=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Original feasible set restricted to D

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-containment implication is mathematically correct and the certificate kind fits, but no source is supplied for the required checkable relaxation-infeasibility certificate or its validity conditions.

children.title: Propagation Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Contradictions exposed by valid domain propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Infeasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite sequence of sound domain reductions ending in an empty variable or constraint domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D^0\) be a search-node domain and let \(D^{t+1}=T_t(D^t)\) for \(t=0,\ldots,q-1\), where every propagation operator is solution-preserving: \(F\cap D^t\subseteq D^{t+1}\subseteq D^t\). A propagation infeasibility certificate records the operators and their premises and ends with \(D^q=\varnothing\), for example because some variable interval has an empty intersection or a constraint range cannot contain its required value. The recorded inclusions and final contradiction certify \(F\cap D^0=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sound propagation preserves every feasible point. If a checkable sequence of such reductions reaches an empty domain, the original search node is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: Each propagation operator has a checkable solution-preservation justification.
The final empty-domain contradiction is exactly verifiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^q=\varnothing\Longrightarrow F\cap D^0=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The solution-preserving reduction implication is coherent and locally appropriate, but the checkability and soundness requirements are operator-specific and have no authoritative cited locator.

children.title: Exhaustive Disjunctive Infeasibility
children.top_down_role: Infeasibility established by resolving every discrete and spatial branch.

knowledge_statements.title: Exhaustive Disjunctive Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite branch-and-bound infeasibility certificate for a bounded MINLP search domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the original feasible set be \(F\), and let \(D_1,\ldots,D_N\) be the terminal branch regions generated by discrete branching and spatial partitioning. Suppose \(F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\), and for every \(i\) a valid relaxation \(R_i\supseteq F\cap D_i\) has been proved infeasible. Then \(F=\varnothing\). The finite collection consisting of the exhaustive-cover description and the independently checkable infeasibility certificates for all \(R_i\) is a global infeasibility certificate for the MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If terminal branches cover the entire search domain and a valid relaxation proves every branch infeasible, their finite collection certifies global infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(N<\infty\).
\(F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^N D_i\).
\(F\cap D_i\subseteq R_i=\varnothing\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\varnothing\).

children.title: Continuous-Relaxation Hardness
children.top_down_role: Hardness inherited from global solution of continuous nonconvex relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Relaxation Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hardness transfer from continuous nonconvex optimization to unrestricted global MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider any class \(\mathcal C\) of continuous nonconvex optimization problems. Form an MINLP class \(\mathcal M\) that permits instances with no integer variables and contains every instance of \(\mathcal C\) unchanged. The identity map is a polynomial-time, objective-preserving reduction from \(\mathcal C\) to \(\mathcal M\). Consequently, if globally solving \(\mathcal C\), or deciding whether its optimum is at most a given threshold, is NP-hard, then the corresponding global MINLP task for \(\mathcal M\) is NP-hard even before discrete branching is introduced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global MINLP inherits the hardness of continuous nonconvex optimization because the latter is its zero-integer-variable special case.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) admits zero integer variables.
\(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal M\) under an encoding-preserving identity map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal C\text{ NP-hard}\implies\mathcal M\text{ NP-hard}.\)

children.title: Discrete-Spatial Complexity Coupling
children.top_down_role: Compounding of discrete enumeration and continuous-domain refinement.

children.title: Combinatorial Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity arising from discrete choices and integer-feasible configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case enumeration cost contributed by binary decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an MINLP with \(p\) binary variables, the discrete domain is \(\{0,1\}^p\) and contains \(2^p\) assignments. An exhaustive algorithm that certifies feasibility, infeasibility, or optimality by separately resolving every assignment therefore solves at most \(2^p\) continuous subproblems. If no valid dominance, propagation, symmetry, or relaxation argument eliminates an unresolved assignment, its worst-case number of discrete leaves is exactly \(2^p\). Thus exhaustive discrete resolution is exponential in the number of binary variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With p binary variables, exhaustive discrete resolution can require all 2^p assignments, independently of the work needed for each continuous subproblem.
assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb N\).
Each unresolved binary assignment requires a separate continuous subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{leaves}}\le 2^p\), with equality possible in the absence of pruning.

notation.meaning: Number of terminal discrete leaves resolved.

children.title: Spatial Refinement Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity arising from continuous-domain partitioning and relaxation refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Refinement Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform spatial complexity for Lipschitz optimization on a bounded box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty bounded box, let \(D=\max_j(b_j-a_j)\), and let \(f:B\to\mathbb R\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz in the infinity norm, with \(L>0\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), partition coordinate interval \([a_j,b_j]\) into \(m_j=\max\{1,\lceil (b_j-a_j)L/\varepsilon\rceil\}\) subintervals and select one point from each Cartesian product cell. The resulting sample set \(G\) has cardinality \(|G|\le(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\), and every \(x\in B\) is within infinity-norm distance at most \(\varepsilon/L\) of a point in \(G\). Therefore, if \(\hat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{g\in G}f(g)\), then \(f(\hat x)-\min_{x\in B}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partitioning a bounded n-dimensional box into cells of side length at most epsilon/L and evaluating one representative per cell gives additive error at most epsilon using at most (1+LD/epsilon)^n evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(B=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]\) is a nonempty bounded box.
\(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|_\infty\) for all \(x,y\in B\).
\(L>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{eval}}\le(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\) and \(f(\hat x)-\min_{x\in B}f(x)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Maximum side length of the box.
Finite set containing one representative from each partition cell.

source_witnesses.locator: Part Two. Partition Strategies in Global Optimization: The Continuous and the Lipschitzian Case p. 39

children.title: Complexity Compounding
children.top_down_role: Regimes where discrete enumeration amplifies spatial-search burden.

knowledge_statements.title: Complexity Compounding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product bound for exhaustive binary enumeration and Lipschitz spatial refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\). For every \(y\in Y\), let the continuous feasible set \(X_y\) lie in an \(n\)-dimensional box of maximum side length at most \(D\), and suppose \(f(y,\cdot)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the infinity norm on that box. Assume that for every \(\varepsilon>0\) one can construct a feasible sample set \(G_y\subseteq X_y\) with \(|G_y|\le(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\) such that every \(x\in X_y\) has some \(g\in G_y\) satisfying \(\|x-g\|_\infty\le\varepsilon/L\). Enumerating all \(y\in Y\) and evaluating every point in every \(G_y\) uses at most \(2^p(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\) evaluations and returns an objective value within \(\varepsilon\) of the global optimum. Thus the discrete and spatial evaluation counts compound multiplicatively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When each continuous feasible branch has an epsilon/L feasible cover of size at most (1+LD/epsilon)^n, exhaustive binary enumeration gives an additive-epsilon solution using at most 2^p times that many evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\).
Each \(X_y\) lies in an \(n\)-box of maximum side length at most \(D\).
Each \(f(y,\cdot)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz in the infinity norm.
Each nonempty \(X_y\) admits the stated feasible \(\varepsilon/L\)-cover \(G_y\).
\(L>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{eval}}\le 2^p(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\), with additive objective error at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Continuous feasible set for binary assignment y.
Finite feasible cover of branch y.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Tractable Subclasses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial solvability under fixed discrete dimension and polynomially solvable continuous branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an MINLP have a fixed number \(p\) of binary variables. Assume that fixing any binary assignment produces a continuous optimization problem solvable globally in time \(T(s)\), polynomial in the encoded instance size \(s\). Enumerating the \(2^p\) assignments, rejecting infeasible branches, and selecting the least feasible objective value solves the MINLP globally in time \(O(2^pT(s))\). Because \(p\) is fixed, this running time is polynomial in \(s\). This subclass includes formulations whose fixed-assignment problems are polynomially solvable convex programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If binary dimension is fixed and every fixed-assignment continuous problem is polynomially solvable, complete enumeration gives a polynomial-time global algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) is constant rather than part of the asymptotic input.
Each fixed-assignment subproblem is globally solvable in polynomial time.
Input encodings and feasibility decisions are exact or polynomially controlled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{MINLP}}(s)=O(2^pT(s))=\operatorname{poly}(s)\).

children.title: Approximation Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive approximation by enumeration and feasible Lipschitz discretization on compact domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\), and for each \(y\in Y\) let \(X_y\) be a compact feasible subset of an \(n\)-dimensional box whose maximum side length is at most \(D\). Suppose \(f(y,\cdot)\) is uniformly \(L\)-Lipschitz. Assume that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), each nonempty \(X_y\) has a computable finite set \(G_y\subseteq X_y\) satisfying \(|G_y|\le(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\) and such that every \(x\in X_y\) is within infinity-norm distance \(\varepsilon/L\) of some \(g\in G_y\). Enumerating \(Y\) and all sets \(G_y\), then returning the best sampled feasible point \((\hat y,\hat x)\), yields \(f(\hat y,\hat x)\le f^*+\varepsilon\) after at most \(2^p(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\) objective evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact Lipschitz MINLP branches admit the stated additive approximation when each feasible set has a computable feasible epsilon/L cover of controlled cardinality.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\).
Each \(X_y\) is compact and lies in a bounded \(n\)-box of maximum side length at most \(D\).
\(f(y,\cdot)\) is uniformly \(L\)-Lipschitz.
Each nonempty \(X_y\) admits the stated computable feasible cover \(G_y\).
\(L>0\) and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\hat y,\hat x)-f^*\le\varepsilon\) using at most \(2^p(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\) objective evaluations.

notation.meaning: Global optimal value over all feasible branches.
Continuous feasible set for assignment y.
Computable feasible cover of branch y.

children.title: Inapproximability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structured subclasses subject to approximation hardness.

knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional approximation hardness obtained from a polynomial objective gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be an NP-complete decision class and suppose a polynomial reduction maps each instance \(I\) to an MINLP with nonnegative optimum \(v(I)\) satisfying \(v(I)=0\) for yes-instances and \(v(I)\ge\Delta(I)>0\) for no-instances, where \(\Delta(I)\) is polynomial-time computable. Any polynomial-time algorithm guaranteeing additive error strictly below \(\Delta(I)/2\) would distinguish the two cases by testing whether its returned value is below \(\Delta(I)/2\). Therefore no such approximation algorithm exists unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomially encoded zero-versus-positive objective gap rules out additive approximation finer than half the gap unless P equals NP.
assumptions_latex: The reduction is polynomial-time and encoding preserving.
\(v(I)=0\) on yes-instances and \(v(I)\ge\Delta(I)>0\) on no-instances.
The approximation returns a feasible value within additive error less than \(\Delta(I)/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{Such a polynomial-time approximation}\implies\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}.\)

children.title: Structured-Subclass Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural transitions separating approximable cases from harder regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured-Subclass Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between fixed-dimensional approximation and dimension-driven exponential growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For compact Lipschitz MINLPs treated by exhaustive binary enumeration and uniform spatial discretization, the evaluation bound is \(2^p(1+LD/\varepsilon)^n\). If \(p\) and \(n\) are fixed constants and \(L\) and \(D\) are polynomially bounded, this bound is polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). If either \(p\) or \(n\) is part of the input, the same guarantee becomes exponential in that dimension. Hence fixed discrete and continuous dimensions define a tractable approximation boundary for this method, not a polynomial guarantee for unrestricted MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumeration-grid approximation is polynomial in inverse accuracy only at fixed discrete and continuous dimensions; variable dimensions restore exponential dependence.
assumptions_latex: The compact-domain Lipschitz grid bound applies.
\(L\) and \(D\) have polynomially controlled magnitudes.
Complexity counts objective or relaxation evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p,n=O(1)\) gives polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\); variable \(p\) or \(n\) gives exponential dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Missing or Weak Variable Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bilinear envelopes require finite factor bounds and weaken as boxes enlarge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w=xy\) with finite bounds \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), the McCormick relaxation is defined by \(w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y\), \(w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y\), \(w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y\), and \(w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y\). These finite affine inequalities require finite endpoints. The maximum vertical separation between the McCormick concave and convex envelope surfaces is \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/2\). Consequently, widening either factor interval can make this relaxation gap arbitrarily large, while an infinite required endpoint makes the standard bounded-box envelope unavailable as a finite affine formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard McCormick envelope needs finite factor bounds, and the maximum separation between its upper and lower envelope surfaces equals half the product of the interval widths.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x,u_x,\ell_y,u_y\in\mathbb R\), with \(\ell_x\le u_x\) and \(\ell_y\le u_y\).
The relaxation is the standard bounded-box McCormick relaxation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The envelope requires finite endpoints, and its maximum vertical width is \((u_x-\ell_x)(u_y-\ell_y)/2\).

children.title: Reformulation-Dependent Relaxation Pathologies

children.title: Expression Dependency
children.top_down_role: Relaxation weakness caused by repeated or coupled expression occurrences.

knowledge_statements.title: Expression Dependency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Natural interval relaxation can lose equality between repeated occurrences of one variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[-1,1]\) and consider \(e(x)=x-x\). Its exact range is \(\{0\}\), whereas occurrence-independent natural interval evaluation gives \([-1,1]-[-1,1]=[-2,2]\). Thus the interval image strictly contains the exact image because the evaluation loses the dependency between the two occurrences of \(x\). More generally, on a subinterval \([a,b]\), the same evaluation gives \([a,b]-[a,b]=[a-b,b-a]\); hence, if this unchanged natural interval evaluation is used, subdivision reduces the overestimation as the subinterval width \(b-a\) decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Although x−x is identically zero, occurrence-independent interval evaluation on [−1,1] returns [−2,2]. Under the same evaluation rule, narrowing the interval reduces this dependency overestimation.
assumptions_latex: Each occurrence is evaluated by ordinary interval arithmetic without dependency tracking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(x-x)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-2,2]\).

notation.meaning: Expression containing two dependent occurrences of x.
A subinterval used for natural interval evaluation.

children.title: Reformulation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in relaxation behavior caused by alternative algebraic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraically equivalent square epigraph formulations can yield different factorable relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(x\in[-1,1]\), the direct epigraph constraint \(w\ge x^2\) is convex. An algebraically equivalent lifted formulation introduces \(y\in[-1,1]\) and imposes \(y=x\) together with \(w\ge xy\). Replacing \(xy\) by its McCormick convex underestimator on \([-1,1]^2\) yields the inequalities \(w\ge-x-y-1\) and \(w\ge x+y-1\). At \(x=y=0\), these inequalities permit \(w=-1\), whereas the direct epigraph requires \(w\ge0\). Hence algebraically equivalent formulations can have different continuous relaxations, and duplicating a variable before constructing a factorable relaxation can strictly weaken the lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The square epigraph is equivalent to a lifted bilinear epigraph with y=x, but its McCormick underestimator permits w=−1 at zero while the direct convex epigraph requires w≥0.
assumptions_latex: The lifted formulation imposes \(y=x\) and \(w\ge xy\).
The bilinear epigraph is relaxed using the McCormick convex underestimator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x,y,w)=(0,0,-1)\) satisfies the lifted McCormick relaxation but violates \(w\ge x^2\).

notation.meaning: Duplicate variable constrained to equal x.

children.title: Equivalent-Form Relaxation Gaps
children.top_down_role: Strength differences among relaxations of algebraically equivalent formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Form Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines formulation dependence after projecting relaxations into the original variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two formulations be equivalent when their feasible sets have the same projection \(F\subseteq X\) onto the original variables. For a minimization objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), let \(R_1,R_2\supseteq F\) be the projected feasible sets produced by a fixed relaxation construction applied to the two formulations. An equivalent-form relaxation gap occurs when \[\inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)\ne\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x).\] Thus algebraic equivalence of the exact formulations does not imply equality of their relaxation bounds. Commutation of the relaxation construction with the reformulation and projection is a sufficient structural condition for equality, but it is not necessary for equality in a particular instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent exact formulations can yield different lower bounds when their constructed relaxations have different projections onto the original variables.
assumptions_latex: \(F\ne\varnothing\) and both exact formulations project to \(F\).
The two relaxation infima are well-defined in \(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in R_1}f(x)\ne\inf_{x\in R_2}f(x)\) identifies formulation-dependent relaxation strength.

notation.meaning: Exact feasible set in the original variables.
Projected relaxation obtained from formulation i.

review_flags: specialized reformulation-relaxation claim requires a direct source

children.title: High-Arity Nonlinear Interactions
children.top_down_role: Relaxation degradation for highly coupled products and composites.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Arity Nonlinear Interactions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies degradation of relaxations for nonlinear terms coupling many variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:B\to\mathbb R\) be a nonlinear term on a box \(B\subset\mathbb R^n\), and let \(R_h(B)\) be a convex relaxation of its graph. Define its vertical relaxation error by \[\Delta_h(B)=\sup\{|w-h(x)|:(x,w)\in R_h(B)\}.\] For a family \(h_n\) whose number of coupled arguments grows, high-arity degradation occurs when there are boxes \(B_n\) of uniformly bounded diameter for which \(\Delta_{h_n}(B_n)\) fails to approach zero, or increases with \(n\). Branching or factorization is then required to recover a prescribed relaxation accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A high-arity interaction is problematic when its graph relaxation remains loose, or becomes looser, as the number of coupled variables grows.
assumptions_latex: Each \(h_n\) is finite on its box \(B_n\).
Each \(R_{h_n}(B_n)\) contains the graph of \(h_n\) over \(B_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Persistent positive \(\Delta_{h_n}(B_n)\) marks a relaxation failure boundary for increasing interaction arity.

notation.meaning: Convex graph relaxation of h on B.

review_flags: metric and arity-dependent boundary need direct factorable-programming evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed arity-dependent error criterion is specialized and not supported by a citation. Uniformly bounded box diameter does not by itself isolate degradation caused by arity, and the assertion that branching or factorization is required excludes other relaxation-strengthening mechanisms.

children.title: Singular-Domain Primitive Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Discontinuities, poles, and restricted primitive domains.

children.title: Singular Primitives
children.top_down_role: Primitive expressions exhibiting poles, blowups, or singular evaluation points.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Primitives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers primitives that become unbounded near points in or on the boundary of a node domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primitive \(\phi:D\to\mathbb R\) and a search box \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a point \(a\in\overline{B\cap D}\) is singular relative to \(B\) if \[\limsup_{x\to a,\,x\in B\cap D}|\phi(x)|=+\infty.\] The primitive is singular on \(B\) when such a point exists. Standard instances include reciprocal expressions approaching a zero denominator and logarithms approaching zero from the positive side. No finite interval image or finite Lipschitz bound for \(\phi\) on \(B\cap D\) can then be asserted without separating the box from the singular boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primitive is singular on a box when its magnitude becomes unbounded near a point approachable from the valid part of the box.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the real-valued domain of \(\phi\).
\(B\cap D\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of such \(a\) makes \(\phi\) singular relative to \(B\).
review_flags: direct source for singular factorable primitives remains required

children.title: Domain-Restricted Primitives
children.top_down_role: Primitive expressions whose admissible inputs occupy restricted domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Restricted Primitives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States real-domain predicates required by common nonlinear primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factorable expression is real-valued only where every primitive-domain predicate is satisfied. In particular, \(\log u\) requires \(u>0\), \(\sqrt{u}\) requires \(u\ge 0\), \(u/v\) requires \(v\ne0\), and \(u^p\) for a noninteger real exponent \(p\) is ordinarily restricted to \(u>0\) under the real principal-value convention. For a search region \(B\), validity of interval evaluation throughout the node requires that the corresponding predicate hold for every \(x\in B\); otherwise the node must be contracted, partitioned, or treated with explicit domain constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logarithms, roots, division, and noninteger powers impose domain predicates that must hold throughout any box evaluated as a whole.
assumptions_latex: All expressions are interpreted over the real numbers.
Primitive arguments \(u\) and \(v\) are functions of \(x\in B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\subseteq D_\phi\) is required for an everywhere-defined real evaluation of primitive \(\phi\) on \(B\).
review_flags: supplied sources lack a locator for primitive-domain propagation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and common real-domain predicates fit the leaf, but the noninteger-power convention and the prescribed node-handling consequences require a specific source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Discontinuity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Evaluation boundaries associated with jumps or undefined limiting behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies boundaries across which continuous relaxation models cannot remain exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=D^-\cup D^+\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), with sequences from both subsets converging to \(a\in\overline{D^-}\cap\overline{D^+}\). A primitive \(\phi:D\to\mathbb R\) has a jump boundary at \(a\) if finite one-sided limits exist and satisfy \[\lim_{x\to a,\,x\in D^-}\phi(x)\ne\lim_{x\to a,\,x\in D^+}\phi(x).\] Any search box intersecting both sides contains a discontinuous graph segment. Consequently, a continuous local model spanning that box cannot represent the primitive exactly; valid global treatment requires disjunction, branching, or a relaxation containing both limiting branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Across a jump boundary, one continuous local model cannot exactly represent both sides of the primitive.
assumptions_latex: Both one-sided approach sets are nonempty near \(a\).
The stated one-sided limits are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unequal one-sided limits make \(a\) a discontinuity boundary requiring branch-aware treatment.

notation.meaning: Two domain sides approaching the boundary.

review_flags: optimization consequence needs a direct deterministic-global-optimization source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The jump-boundary definition is mathematically coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits, but the required global-optimization treatments are not established by any cited source.

children.title: Domain Violation Consequences
children.top_down_role: Relaxation, search, or certification effects caused by invalid primitive evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Violation Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates infeasibility certification from inconclusive or invalid primitive evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a constraint contain a primitive \(\phi(g(x))\) with exact real domain \(D_\phi\), let \(B\) be a search box, let \(g[B]=\{g(x):x\in B\}\) be the exact argument image, and let \(I_g(B)\supseteq g[B]\) be a computed enclosure. If \(I_g(B)\cap D_\phi=\varnothing\), then \(g[B]\cap D_\phi=\varnothing\), so every point of \(B\) violates the expression domain and the box is infeasible. If \(g[B]\) contains both valid and invalid argument values, evaluating \(\phi\) over the whole image is not an everywhere-defined finite evaluation. If only \(I_g(B)\) overlaps both sides of the domain boundary, the enclosure is inconclusive: the box must be contracted, partitioned, more tightly enclosed, or handled with explicit domain modeling before domain validity can support certified pruning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An enclosure wholly outside a primitive's domain certifies infeasibility, while an enclosure straddling the domain boundary is merely inconclusive unless actual invalid argument values are established.
assumptions_latex: \(D_\phi\) is the exact real domain of \(\phi\).
\(I_g(B)\supseteq g[B]=\{g(x):x\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_g(B)\cap D_\phi=\varnothing\) certifies domain infeasibility, whereas overlap of \(I_g(B)\) with both \(D_\phi\) and its complement does not by itself certify mixed validity of the exact image.

notation.meaning: Exact real domain of the primitive.
Exact argument image over the box.
Computed enclosure containing the exact argument image.

review_flags: certification consequences require a source specific to interval or spatial branch-and-bound methods

children.title: Search-Certification Reliability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which search progress or reported certification becomes unreliable.

children.title: Relaxation-Gap Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Persistent bound gaps under ineffective refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Gap Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines persistent failure of node refinement to close certified bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a nested sequence of branch-and-bound regions \(B_{k+1}\subseteq B_k\), valid lower bounds \(L_k\), and incumbent upper bounds \(U_k\), with \(L_k\le f^*_{B_k}\le U_k\). Relaxation-gap stagnation occurs along the sequence if refinement continues but \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}(U_k-L_k)>0.\] Under an absolute termination tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), a stagnation level exceeding \(\varepsilon\) prevents this branch from being certified by the gap test. Causes may include nonconvergent relaxations, ineffective branching, or an incumbent that is not improved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gap stagnation occurs when valid upper and lower bounds remain separated by a positive amount despite continuing refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(L_k\) and \(U_k\) are valid bounds for the same node subproblem.
The bounds are measured on a common objective scale.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\liminf_k(U_k-L_k)>\varepsilon\), the absolute-gap stopping test cannot certify the branch.

notation.meaning: Certified lower bound and incumbent upper bound at refinement k.
Optimal value restricted to the current region.

review_flags: formal stagnation criterion is standard but not supported by supplied locators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The criterion is internally coherent and the failure-boundary kind fits, but this formal definition of stagnation and its stated causes have no supporting locator or citation.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Symmetry
children.top_down_role: Equivalent discrete or spatial regions causing redundant search.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines objective- and feasibility-preserving symmetries in mixed-integer models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a mixed-integer feasible set \(F\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\), a symmetry is a bijection \(\sigma:F\to F\) satisfying \(f(\sigma(x))=f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). A symmetry group \(G\) partitions \(F\) into orbits \(Gx=\{\sigma(x):\sigma\in G\}\). Searching two distinct points or subregions in the same orbit is redundant for objective-value certification. A valid symmetry-breaking restriction retains at least one representative from every feasible orbit and therefore preserves the global optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mixed-integer symmetry maps feasible solutions bijectively to equal-valued feasible solutions, creating redundant search across each orbit.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) is nonempty.
Every \(\sigma\in G\) preserves feasibility and objective value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Retaining at least one point from every orbit preserves \(\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).
review_flags: mixed-integer symmetry definition needs a directly relevant source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The group-orbit definition and optimal-value preservation statement are mathematically coherent and appropriately classified as a definition, but no mixed-integer symmetry source is supplied.

children.title: Fragmented Feasible-Region Geometry
children.top_down_role: Geometries that impede incumbent generation and local repair.

children.title: Disconnected Feasible Components
children.top_down_role: Separated feasible components that obstruct movement between candidate regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Feasible Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses relative topology within the mixed-integer search domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) carry the subspace topology inherited from \(\mathbb R^{p+q}\), and let \(F\subseteq X\) be feasible. The set \(F\) is disconnected when there exist nonempty disjoint sets \(F_1,F_2\subseteq F\), both open in the relative topology of \(F\), such that \(F=F_1\cup F_2\). Its connected components are the maximal connected subsets of \(F\). The image of any continuous feasible path is connected, so such a path cannot join points in different connected components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible set is disconnected when it admits a separation into two nonempty disjoint relatively open parts; its connected components are its maximal connected subsets, and no continuous feasible path joins different components.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) has the relative topology inherited from \(\mathbb R^{p+q}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A separation \(F=F_1\cup F_2\) with the stated properties makes \(F\) disconnected.

notation.meaning: Nonempty relatively open parts forming a separation.

review_flags: an exact topology or optimization locator remains required

children.title: Thin Feasible Regions
children.top_down_role: Low-volume or nearly lower-dimensional feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Thin Feasible Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines geometric thinness through relative inradius inside a search region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), where \(B\) is a bounded search region. The feasible set is \(\delta\)-thin in \(B\) if its inradius \[r(F;B)=\sup\{r\ge0:\exists x\in F\text{ with }\overline{B}(x,r)\cap B\subseteq F\}\] satisfies \(r(F;B)\le\delta\). If \(r(F;B)=0\), then \(F\) contains no positive-radius ball relative to \(B\), as occurs for many equality-defined feasible manifolds. Sampling or perturbation methods requiring a full-dimensional feasible neighborhood then have no uniform positive-radius target.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible region is thin when it contains no relative ball larger than a prescribed small radius.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and \(F\subseteq B\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r(F;B)\le\delta\) defines \(\delta\)-thinness within \(B\).

notation.meaning: Relative inradius of the feasible set within B.
Closed Euclidean ball centered at x with radius r.

review_flags: chosen quantitative notion of thinness needs direct source alignment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed relative-inradius definition is coherent and fits the geometric leaf, but it is a selected quantitative meaning of thinness rather than a uniquely standard definition. Direct source alignment is required.

children.title: Incumbent Access Barriers
children.top_down_role: Geometric conditions that impede discovery of feasible incumbents.

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent Access Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when a search mechanism cannot reach a better feasible component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be partitioned into feasible components, let \(x^I\in F\) be the current incumbent, and let \(\mathcal R(x^I)\subseteq F\) be all feasible points reachable by the algorithm's permitted local moves and repairs. An incumbent access barrier exists when \[\inf_{x\in F}f(x)<\inf_{x\in\mathcal R(x^I)}f(x).\] Then no sequence of those permitted operations starting from \(x^I\) can produce a globally optimal incumbent. Certification may still proceed through valid lower bounds, but incumbent improvement requires a nonlocal start, branching into another component, or an expanded move set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An access barrier exists when all solutions reachable from the incumbent are worse than the global optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(x^I\in F\) is feasible.
\(\mathcal R(x^I)\) exactly represents reachability under the specified algorithmic moves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A strict reachable-set value gap prevents the permitted local mechanism from reaching a global minimizer.

notation.meaning: Feasible points reachable by permitted moves.

review_flags: algorithm-relative barrier formulation requires direct heuristic-search evidence

children.title: Local Repair Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Feasible-region geometries under which local repair becomes unreliable.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Repair Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a distance boundary beyond which bounded local repair cannot restore feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed, let \(y\in X\) be an infeasible trial point, and suppose a local repair operator may return only points in \(X\cap\overline{B}(y,\rho)\). If \[\operatorname{dist}(y,F)=\inf_{x\in F}\|x-y\|>\rho,\] then the permitted repair neighborhood contains no feasible point, so every such repair must fail. Likewise, if repair moves are constrained to a connected neighborhood that does not intersect another feasible component, they cannot access that component. Success therefore requires enlarging the radius, changing neighborhoods, or invoking a nonlocal feasibility mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radius-limited repair must fail whenever the nearest feasible point lies beyond its allowed neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty and closed.
The repair output is constrained to \(\overline{B}(y,\rho)\cap X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(y,F)>\rho\) certifies failure of every repair obeying the radius limit.

notation.meaning: Distance from the trial point to feasibility.

review_flags: geometric claim is elementary but local-repair interpretation needs a relevant source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The radius-distance implication is mathematically correct and the failure-boundary kind fits, but its interpretation as a local-repair boundary and the component-level extension lack a relevant source.

children.title: Numerical Tolerance Conflicts
children.top_down_role: Conflicts among integrality, feasibility, bounding, and optimality tolerances.

assumptions_latex: The original MINLP is \(\min\{f(x):g(x)\le 0,\ x\in X,\ x_I\in\mathbb Z^{|I|}\}\), with exact feasible set \(F\).
The reported incumbent value is \(U=f(\hat x)\) and the reported global lower bound is \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}|U|\) is a valid global-optimality certificate only when \(\hat x\in F\) and \(L\le \inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) are independently certified under compatible tolerances.

notation.meaning: Exact feasible set of the MINLP.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a numerical gap test cannot certify global optimality unless feasibility, integrality, and bound validity are established under compatible error conventions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional MINLP certification with absolute and relative gap tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau_f,\tau_I,\tau_b\ge 0\) denote feasibility, integrality, and bound-validity error allowances. A tolerance conflict occurs when the solver applies the gap test \(U-L\le \varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}|U|\) although either \(\hat x\notin F\), an integer component satisfies only \(\operatorname{dist}(\hat x_I,\mathbb Z^{|I|})\le\tau_I\) without an exactly feasible repair, or the computed bound may exceed the true optimum by \(\tau_b\). In any such case, the displayed gap alone is not a rigorous certificate. A valid certificate requires a certified feasible incumbent and a certified lower bound, with all numerical errors included in the final gap inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small reported gap is not conclusive when incumbent feasibility, integrality, or lower-bound validity uses incompatible tolerances. Certification requires a truly feasible incumbent and a rigorous bound with numerical errors included.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Tolerance Conflicts

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but the interaction among feasibility, integrality, bound-validity, and gap tolerances has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Nonrigorous Subsolver Status
children.top_down_role: Loss of certification when local or numerical statuses are treated as globally conclusive.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonrigorous Subsolver Status
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes numerical termination labels from verifiable deterministic global-search certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a subsolver returns a label such as locally optimal, stationary, numerically infeasible, iteration limit, or feasible. Such a label is not by itself a global certificate. A search region \(B\) may be pruned after a verifiable proof that \(F\cap B=\varnothing\), or after establishing a valid lower bound \(L_B\le\inf_{x\in F\cap B}f(x)\) and comparing it with a certified feasible incumbent value \(U\), for example through \(L_B\ge U\) for exact pruning or \(L_B\ge U-\varepsilon\) for an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate. Declaring global optimality additionally requires that all remaining regions be covered by such valid conclusions. Treating an unsupported local or floating-point status as one of these implications can discard a region containing a better feasible point and destroys deterministic global certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local optimality, heuristic feasibility, or numerical infeasibility does not justify global pruning. Pruning requires certified regional infeasibility or a valid regional lower bound that is sufficiently large relative to a certified feasible incumbent.
assumptions_latex: The problem is a minimization MINLP with exact feasible set \(F\) and optimal value \(v^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).
A certified feasible incumbent has value \(U\), and a global-search node corresponds to a region \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A subsolver status is globally conclusive only when it verifies an implication such as \(F\cap B=\varnothing\), or verifies \(L_B\le\inf_{x\in F\cap B}f(x)\) together with the incumbent comparison required for pruning.

notation.meaning: Exact feasible set and global optimal value.
Certified lower bound over the current region.
Value of a certified feasible incumbent.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: deterministic pruning requires certified infeasibility or a valid regional bound compared with a certified incumbent

children.title: Source-Based Pooling Formulations
children.top_down_role: Pooling representations organized by source contributions.

assumptions_latex: Sources are indexed by \(i\in S\), pools by \(\ell\in P\), terminals by \(j\in T\), and qualities by \(k\in K\).
Each source quality \(a_{ik}\) is fixed, and all flows are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The source-indexed variables expose each terminal quality mass as \(\sum_i a_{ik}(d_{ij}+\sum_\ell w_{i\ell j})\) while enforcing common pool composition through \(w_{i\ell j}=q_{i\ell}y_{\ell j}\).

notation.meaning: Fraction of pool inflow originating at source i.
Flow from pool l to terminal j and its source-i contribution.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: source-based pooling disaggregates pool-to-terminal flow by source and links contributions through common pool proportions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous source-based formulation for a standard source-pool-terminal network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A source-based pooling representation introduces proportions \(q_{i\ell}\ge0\) and source contributions \(w_{i\ell j}\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum_i q_{i\ell}=1\), \(w_{i\ell j}=q_{i\ell}y_{\ell j}\), and \(\sum_i w_{i\ell j}=y_{\ell j}\). If \(x_{i\ell}\) is source-to-pool flow, source conservation at a pool is \(\sum_j w_{i\ell j}=x_{i\ell}\) when the pool has no accumulation or loss. Terminal flow and quality mass are respectively \(\sum_i d_{ij}+\sum_{i,\ell}w_{i\ell j}\) and \(\sum_i a_{ik}(d_{ij}+\sum_\ell w_{i\ell j})\). The only displayed nonconvexities are the common-composition products.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Source-based pooling tracks how much of every terminal delivery originated at each source. Bilinear equations force all outgoing arcs of a pool to share the same source proportions.
knowledge_statements.title: Source-Based Pooling Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the source-based leaf, but its exact disaggregation and conservation equations require a pooling-specific source with a precise locator.

children.title: Pool-Based Pooling Formulations
children.top_down_role: Pooling representations organized by intermediate pools.

assumptions_latex: Sources, pools, terminals, and qualities are finite sets \(S,P,T,K\).
Pool \(\ell\) is perfectly mixed, has no accumulation, and has quality \(p_{\ell k}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Perfect mixing is represented by the pool balance \(p_{\ell k}\sum_i x_{i\ell}=\sum_i a_{ik}x_{i\ell}\), and outgoing quality mass on arc \((\ell,j)\) equals \(p_{\ell k}y_{\ell j}\).

notation.meaning: Quality k of material in pool l.
Fixed quality k of source i.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pool-based pooling uses pool qualities and bilinear quality-flow products on pool arcs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect-mixing pool-quality formulation without losses or inventory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pool-based formulation associates each pool \(\ell\) with total flow balance \(\sum_i x_{i\ell}=\sum_j y_{\ell j}\) and quality variables \(p_{\ell k}\). Perfect mixing requires \(p_{\ell k}\sum_i x_{i\ell}=\sum_i a_{ik}x_{i\ell}\) for every quality \(k\). The quality mass delivered from pool \(\ell\) to terminal \(j\) is \(p_{\ell k}y_{\ell j}\), so terminal quality specifications are linear in direct-source quality masses and these bilinear pool contributions. The formulation is organized around one composition vector per pool; consequently every outgoing pool arc automatically carries that same composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pool-based pooling assigns one quality vector to each perfectly mixed pool. Bilinear products of pool quality and outgoing flow determine quality mass delivered to terminals.
knowledge_statements.title: Pool-Based Pooling Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pool-quality representation is plausible and appropriately classified as a representation, but no inspectable source supports the exact formulation.

children.title: Terminal-Based Pooling Formulations
children.top_down_role: Pooling representations organized by terminal deliveries.

assumptions_latex: The network contains sources \(S\), pools \(P\), terminals \(T\), and fixed source qualities \(a_{ik}\).
All routed and direct flows are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Terminal specifications can be written directly in delivered-source variables as \(\underline a_{jk}D_j\le\sum_i a_{ik}z_{ij}\le\overline a_{jk}D_j\), with \(D_j=\sum_i z_{ij}\).

notation.meaning: Total amount from source i delivered to terminal j.
Source-i contribution routed through pool l to terminal j.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: terminal-based pooling aggregates deliveries by source at each terminal and imposes terminal specifications on those aggregates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal-delivery disaggregation for a source-pool-terminal pooling network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A terminal-based representation introduces delivered-source amounts \(z_{ij}\ge0\) with \(z_{ij}=d_{ij}+\sum_\ell w_{i\ell j}\) and \(D_j=\sum_i z_{ij}\). For terminal quality interval \([\underline a_{jk},\overline a_{jk}]\), its specification becomes \(\underline a_{jk}D_j\le\sum_i a_{ik}z_{ij}\le\overline a_{jk}D_j\). Routed contributions must also be compatible with a single composition at each pool, for example through \(w_{i\ell j}=q_{i\ell}y_{\ell j}\) and the associated source and pool flow balances. Thus terminal constraints are explicit and linear in delivered-source quantities, while common-composition linking retains the nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Terminal-based pooling aggregates each source's contribution at each terminal. Terminal quality limits become linear in these delivered-source amounts, while pool-consistency equations retain bilinear mixing constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminal-Based Pooling Formulations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed terminal-quality equations are plausible, but the identification of this particular disaggregation as a terminal-based formulation needs a pooling-specific source.

children.title: Pooling Bilinear Quality Structure
children.top_down_role: Bilinear mixing structure linking flows and qualities.

assumptions_latex: Each pool is perfectly mixed and operates at steady state without quality-dependent loss.
Flow and quality variables have finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fundamental nonconvex graph is \(m_{\ell jk}=p_{\ell k}y_{\ell j}\); equivalently, source-disaggregated formulations contain \(w_{i\ell j}=q_{i\ell}y_{\ell j}\).

notation.meaning: Quality-mass flow on a pool-to-terminal arc.
Source fraction and source-specific outgoing contribution.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: perfect mixing multiplies an endogenous composition by an endogenous outgoing flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steady-state perfect mixing with endogenous pool qualities and flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every pool-to-terminal arc and quality, conservation of quality mass gives \(m_{\ell jk}=p_{\ell k}y_{\ell j}\). Both factors are decision variables, so the equality is bilinear and its graph is generally nonconvex whenever both factors vary over nondegenerate intervals. In a source-proportion representation, the same mixing structure appears as \(w_{i\ell j}=q_{i\ell}y_{\ell j}\). Pool flow balance and quality-mass balance couple these products across arcs. If either pool composition or every relevant outgoing flow is fixed, the corresponding products become affine; otherwise global optimization must bound or relax their bilinear graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfect mixing multiplies an endogenous pool quality or source fraction by an outgoing flow. These bilinear equalities create pooling nonconvexity unless one factor is fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Pooling Bilinear Quality Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bilinear perfect-mixing property fits the leaf and is stated coherently, but it lacks an inspectable pooling-specific citation.

children.title: Pooling Relaxation Families
children.top_down_role: Network-flow, bilinear, and strengthened relaxations specialized to pooling.

assumptions_latex: Each bilinear term has the form \(w=xy\) over finite bounds \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\).
All original network flow and quality-mass balances are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strengthened pooling relaxation is \(R_{\mathrm{pool}}=R_{\mathrm{flow}}\cap R_{\mathrm{Mc}}\cap R_{\mathrm{valid}}\), and every valid added inequality preserves containment of the original feasible set.

notation.meaning: Intersection of McCormick envelopes for bilinear terms.
Pooling-specific valid inequalities or lifted constraints.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded bilinear pooling terms admit McCormick envelopes that can be intersected with network-flow and valid-inequality systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex outer relaxations for bounded continuous pooling formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The network-flow relaxation drops common-composition products but retains capacities, conservation, and terminal specifications. For each \(w=xy\), the bilinear relaxation adds the four McCormick inequalities \(w\ge\ell_xy+\ell_yx-\ell_x\ell_y\), \(w\ge u_xy+u_yx-u_xu_y\), \(w\le u_xy+\ell_yx-u_x\ell_y\), and \(w\le\ell_xy+u_yx-\ell_xu_y\). A strengthened pooling relaxation intersects these envelopes with flow equations and pooling-specific valid inequalities, lifted disaggregations, or bound-tightening consequences. Every such constraint must be valid for the original pooling feasible set, so the resulting system remains an outer relaxation and provides a minimization lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pooling relaxations combine network-flow constraints, McCormick envelopes for bounded products, and valid pooling-specific strengthenings. Tighter variable bounds and disaggregation generally strengthen the resulting global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Pooling Relaxation Families

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The McCormick inequalities are correctly formed, but the pooling-specific relaxation family and strengthening claims have no authoritative locator.

children.title: Pooling Topology Regimes
children.top_down_role: Acyclic, cyclic, sparse, and multi-quality pooling networks.

assumptions_latex: A pooling network is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\) with sources, intermediate pools, and terminals.
Each pool may carry one or more quality attributes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is determined by graph cycles, arc sparsity, and quality dimension; these features alter coupling and relaxation structure but not the perfect-mixing conservation laws.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: pooling instances are naturally classified by directed topology, sparsity, and number of qualities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural classification of finite directed pooling networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pooling topology regime is specified by the directed subgraph induced by intermediate pools, its arc density, and the quality dimension. The regime is acyclic when this subgraph has no directed cycle and cyclic otherwise. It is sparse relative to a declared admissible supergraph \((V,A_{\max})\) when \(|A|\ll|A_{\max}|\). It is single-quality when \(|K|=1\) and multi-quality when \(|K|>1\). Cycles permit recirculation and mutually coupled pool compositions; multiple qualities replicate quality-mass equations while sharing the same flows; sparsity restricts which mixing products and paths can occur.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pooling regimes are classified by whether pool connections contain cycles, how sparse the admissible arcs are, and whether one or several qualities share the same flows.
knowledge_statements.title: Pooling Topology Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The structural classification fits the leaf, but the regime taxonomy is unsourced and the condition \(|A|\ll|A_{\max}|\) is qualitative rather than a precise definition.

children.title: Process Synthesis Model Family

children.title: Process Network Models
children.top_down_role: Network-structured process synthesis instances with discrete topology choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Process Network Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steady-state superstructure models for process-network synthesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite process superstructure. A process network model has binary selection variables \(y\in\{0,1\}^m\), continuous operating variables \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), conservation equations \(My+Nx=0\), activation and capacity constraints \(\underline x_a y_a\le x_a\le\overline x_a y_a\) for each optional component \(a\), constitutive equations \(h_r(x,y)=0\) for \(r\in R\), and operational inequalities \(g_s(x,y)\le0\) for \(s\in Q\). The matrices \(M,N\), finite index sets \(R,Q\), bounds, and constraint functions are model data. A feasible point selects a subnetwork of the superstructure and supplies operating variables satisfying all activation, conservation, capacity, constitutive, and operational constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A process network model selects units and connections from a finite superstructure and assigns operating variables satisfying activation logic, conservation, capacities, physical equations, and operational limits.
assumptions_latex: A finite superstructure graph \(G=(V,A)\) describes candidate process units and material or energy connections.
Binary variables indicate selected units or arcs, continuous variables describe operation, and all constraint index sets are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible process networks are exactly the pairs \((y,x)\) satisfying the stated topology-activation, conservation, capacity, constitutive, and operational constraints.

notation.meaning: Finite index sets for constitutive equations and operational inequalities.

children.title: Process Design Models
children.top_down_role: Equipment selection, sizing, or configuration instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Process Design Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded steady-state process design as a nonconvex MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A process design model chooses topology variables \(y\in\{0,1\}^m\), bounded design variables \(d\in D\subset\mathbb R^p\), and bounded operating variables \(x\in X\subset\mathbb R^n\) by solving \[\min_{y,d,x}\; C_f(y)+C_d(d)+C_o(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad H(y,d,x)=0,\quad G(y,d,x)\le0.\] Activation constraints force variables associated with absent units to zero. The equalities express balances and constitutive laws, while the inequalities impose performance, safety, capacity, and product specifications. Nonconvex objective or constraint functions produce a nonconvex MINLP for which certified global optimality requires global search.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A process design model jointly selects equipment and connectivity, sizes the selected equipment, and chooses operating conditions subject to activation, physical, safety, capacity, and product constraints.
assumptions_latex: A process topology is selected by binary variables \(y\in\{0,1\}^m\).
Continuous design variables \(d\in D\subset\mathbb R^p\) and operating variables \(x\in X\subset\mathbb R^n\) have prescribed finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible design is a triple \((y,d,x)\) satisfying activation, physics, and specifications; a globally optimal design minimizes total cost over all such triples.

notation.meaning: Bounded domains for design and operating variables.
