children.title: Nonlinear Physical Couplings
children.top_down_role: Physical relations that create nonconvex coupling across process decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Physical Couplings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic bounded constitutive couplings in steady-state process synthesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded domain and let \(H:D\to\mathbb R^r\) collect the nonlinear physical residuals. Nonlinear physical coupling occurs when two or more endogenous process quantities enter a common constitutive equation nonaffinely. Representative relations include \(q=UA\Delta T_{\mathrm{lm}}\), \(F_i=Fz_i\), and \(y_i=K_i(T,P,x)x_i\). When participating variables range over nondegenerate intervals, products, ratios, logarithms, exponentials, or variable-dependent coefficients can make the set \(\{x\in D:H(x)=0\}\) nonconvex. Shared temperatures, pressures, compositions, and flows transmit these couplings across units through conservation equations, so independently feasible unit calculations need not combine into a feasible network state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process physics can couple flows, compositions, temperatures, pressures, and equipment variables through nonaffine constitutive equations. These shared couplings can create a nonconvex network feasible set and multiple feasible operating states.
assumptions_latex: Process variables lie in a bounded domain \(D\subset\mathbb R^n\).
Conservation equations and constitutive laws are imposed simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coupled nonlinear equalities can define a nonconvex feasible set, so local feasibility or stationarity does not by itself certify a globally optimal process design.

notation.meaning: Bounded domain of physical and design variables.

children.title: Process Synthesis Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Global-search regimes arising in alternative process configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Process Synthesis Search Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic branch-and-bound regime for bounded process-synthesis MINLPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize the active collection as \(\mathcal B=\{B_0\}\) and the certified incumbent value as \(U=+\infty\). For a selected region \(B\in\mathcal B\), solve a valid convex relaxation to obtain \(L_B\), use a feasible process-design subproblem to seek a certified feasible incumbent, and update \(U\) when one is found. Prune \(B\) if it is certified infeasible or if \(U<+\infty\) and \(L_B\ge U-\varepsilon\). Otherwise branch on a discrete decision or partition a bounded nonlinear variable, optionally tighten bounds, and insert the resulting regions. While \(\mathcal B\ne\varnothing\), define the active global lower bound by \(L=\min_{B\in\mathcal B}L_B\). Stop with an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-global certificate when a certified incumbent exists and either \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) or every active region has been validly pruned. The latter case does not require evaluating a minimum over an empty collection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deterministic process-synthesis search alternates valid relaxation bounds, certified feasible-design searches, pruning, and branching. It returns an absolute epsilon-global certificate only after finding a certified incumbent and closing the active global gap or validly pruning every remaining region.
assumptions_latex: The bounded process-synthesis MINLP has objective \(f\), feasible set \(F\), and a finite discrete superstructure.
Every active search region has a valid convex-relaxation lower bound, and every reported incumbent is certified feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If termination occurs with a certified incumbent value \(U\) and either \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) for the active global lower bound \(L\), or all remaining regions have been validly pruned at tolerance \(\varepsilon\), then the incumbent is absolute \(\varepsilon\)-globally optimal.

notation.meaning: Certified incumbent value and active global lower bound.
Active collection of bounded search regions.
Valid lower bound for region B.

children.title: Energy-System Models
children.top_down_role: Discrete operational and design models with nonlinear energy flows.

knowledge_statements.title: Energy-System Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon deterministic design and operation models with bounded continuous and discrete decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[\ell,u]\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a bounded continuous operating domain and let \(Z\subset\mathbb Z^p\) be a finite set of design, installation, commitment, or operating-mode decisions. An energy-system MINLP may be represented as \[\min\{f(x,z):g(x,z)\le 0,\ h(x,z)=0,\ x\in X,\ z\in Z\}.\] Components of \(x\) represent quantities such as generation, storage states, temperatures, pressures, voltages, or flows. Balance equations are included in \(h\), while capacity, reliability, and operating limits are included in \(g\). The model is nonconvex when its continuous relaxation has a nonconvex objective or feasible region, as can occur through nonlinear losses, efficiencies, or network physics.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-horizon energy-system MINLP combines bounded continuous operations with finite discrete design or commitment choices, balance equations, and operating limits. It is nonconvex when the continuous relaxation has a nonconvex objective or feasible region.
assumptions_latex: A finite planning horizon and finite sets of assets, nodes, and operating periods are given.
The continuous domain is a bounded box \(X=[\ell,u]\subset\mathbb R^n\), and the discrete domain is a finite set \(Z\subset\mathbb Z^p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation is a bounded MINLP whose feasible points specify an energy-system design and operating schedule; it is nonconvex when its continuous relaxation has a nonconvex objective or feasible region.

notation.meaning: continuous energy-flow, state, and operating variables
integer design, installation, commitment, or mode variables
bounded continuous domain and finite discrete domain

children.title: Quadratic MINLP Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models dominated by quadratic objectives or constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic MINLP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded mixed-integer models whose objective and constraints have total degree at most two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w=(x,z)\in D=X\times Z\), where \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded and \(Z\subset\mathbb Z^p\) is bounded and contains at least one integer-valued decision component. A quadratic MINLP has an affine-quadratic objective and affine-quadratic constraints, for example \[\min_{w\in D}\;w^{\mathsf T}Q_0w+c_0^{\mathsf T}w+d_0\quad\text{subject to}\quad w^{\mathsf T}Q_iw+c_i^{\mathsf T}w+d_i\le 0,\quad i=1,\ldots,m.\] Each \(Q_i\) may be taken symmetric, and quadratic equalities may be represented by paired inequalities. Its continuous relaxation is nonconvex when the relaxed objective is nonconvex on the relevant feasible domain or the relaxed feasible set is nonconvex; indefinite quadratic terms are a common, but domain-dependent, source of this nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic MINLP has affine-quadratic objectives and constraints over bounded continuous and integer domains. Its continuous relaxation is nonconvex when its objective or feasible region is nonconvex; indefinite quadratic terms are a common possible cause.
assumptions_latex: The continuous domain \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\) is bounded.
The discrete domain \(Z\subset\mathbb Z^p\) is bounded and includes at least one integer-valued decision component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every objective and constraint is affine-quadratic, while integrality and domain-relevant nonconvex quadratic terms may make the continuous relaxation nonconvex.

notation.meaning: combined continuous and integer decision vector

children.title: Higher-Degree Polynomial MINLP Models
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer models containing cubic or higher-degree polynomial structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Degree Polynomial MINLP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded mixed-integer polynomial models having an objective or constraint of total degree greater than two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\in D\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(D\) is bounded and a nonempty coordinate set \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is constrained by \(w_j\in\mathbb Z\) for every \(j\in J\). A polynomial MINLP has the form \[\min\{p_0(w):p_i(w)\le 0,\ i=1,\ldots,m,\ w\in D\},\qquad p_i(w)=\sum_{\alpha\in A_i}c_{i\alpha}w^\alpha,\] where each \(A_i\subset\mathbb N^n\) is finite, every displayed coefficient \(c_{i\alpha}\) is nonzero, \(w^\alpha=\prod_{j=1}^n w_j^{\alpha_j}\), and \(\lvert\alpha\rvert=\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_j\). It is higher-degree when \(\max_{0\le i\le m,\,\alpha\in A_i}\lvert\alpha\rvert>2\) after like terms have been combined. Higher-degree powers and multilinear products can, but need not, produce nonconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-degree polynomial MINLP is a bounded mixed-integer polynomial model whose objective or at least one constraint has total degree greater than two after like terms are combined. Such terms can, but need not, make the model nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: The decision vector satisfies \(w\in D\subset\mathbb R^n\), where \(D\) is bounded.
A nonempty index set \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) identifies coordinates constrained to be integer-valued.
Every objective and constraint is a finite polynomial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation is a higher-degree polynomial MINLP precisely when an objective or constraint contains a nonzero monomial of total degree greater than two after like terms are combined.

children.title: Sparse Algebraic Structures
children.top_down_role: Benchmark structures characterized by limited monomial interaction patterns.

assumptions_latex: The model is polynomial and its variables are indexed by a finite set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Correlative sparsity is represented by a graph or hypergraph whose small interacting variable sets can support decomposed relaxations.

notation.meaning: support of polynomial term or constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable-interaction sparsity in bounded polynomial MINLP formulations.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each monomial or constraint, let \(S_k\) be the set of variables appearing with nonzero exponent or coefficient. The correlative-sparsity graph \(G=(V,E)\) has \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(\{i,j\}\in E\) whenever \(i\ne j\) and \(i,j\in S_k\) for some \(k\). Equivalently, the family \(\{S_k\}\) forms an interaction hypergraph. The model has interaction width \(\omega=\max_k\lvert S_k\rvert\); it is sparse relative to dimension when \(\omega\ll n\) and a chordal extension of \(G\) has maximal cliques much smaller than \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial-model sparsity is encoded by the graph or hypergraph of variables that co-occur in terms or constraints, enabling structure-aware decomposition when interaction sets remain small.

children.title: Algebraic Relaxation Stress Cases
children.top_down_role: Structured instances used to expose relaxation or branching limitations.

assumptions_latex: The variables satisfy \(-1\le x\le1\) and \(0\le y\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing \(y=x^2\) by its convex-hull inequalities admits points absent from the graph, so relaxation feasibility need not imply original feasibility.

notation.meaning: graph of the square function on the bounded interval
convex hull used as a relaxation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete relaxation-gap mechanism for nonlinear algebraic equalities.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 2. Basic Concepts of Global Optimization p. 33

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le1,\ y=x^2\}\). Its convex hull is \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{(x,y):-1\le x\le1,\ x^2\le y\le1\}.\] Thus \((0,1)\in\operatorname{conv}(S)\) although \((0,1)\notin S\). If another constraint enforces \(y=1\), the relaxation permits \(x=0\), whereas the original equality requires \(x\in\{-1,1\}\). Consequently, even the convex hull of an isolated nonlinear graph can produce a strict relaxation after its variables are coupled to other constraints, creating a stress case for node relaxations and branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of a bounded square-function graph contains nongraph points; coupling such a relaxation to other constraints can create a strict feasibility or objective gap.

children.title: Geometric-Network Design Model Family
children.top_down_role: Discrete design models with geometric, distance, or flow-induced nonconvexity.

children.title: Facility Location Models
children.top_down_role: Discrete facility placement instances with nonlinear assignment or distance effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Facility Location Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacitated facility selection with fractional assignment and optional continuous facility locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite set of demand points and \(J\) a finite set of candidate facilities. For \(i\in I\), let \(d_i\ge0\) be demand; for \(j\in J\), let \(F_j\ge0\), \(C_j\ge0\), and bounded \(U_j\subset\mathbb R^d\) denote opening cost, capacity, and the permitted location region. A capacitated facility-location MINLP may be written as \[\min\ \sum_{j\in J}F_jz_j+\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}d_i c_{ij}(u_j)a_{ij}\] subject to \[\sum_{j\in J}a_{ij}=1\quad(i\in I),\qquad 0\le a_{ij}\le z_j,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}d_i a_{ij}\le C_jz_j\quad(j\in J),\] together with \(z_j\in\{0,1\}\) and \(u_j\in U_j\). Here \(a_{ij}\) is the fraction of demand \(i\) assigned to facility \(j\), and \(c_{ij}(u_j)\) is its unit service cost. Fixed candidate locations and constant service costs give a MILP; variable locations or nonlinear distance-dependent costs can yield a nonconvex MINLP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated facility-location model chooses facilities, assigns every demand point within installed capacity, and optionally chooses facility coordinates. Variable locations or nonlinear distance-dependent service costs can make the formulation a nonconvex MINLP.
assumptions_latex: The demand set \(I\) and candidate-facility set \(J\) are finite.

children.top_down_role: Topology-selection instances with nonlinear flow or capacity effects.

assumptions_latex: A finite directed graph, node demands, bounded arc flows, and binary arc-installation decisions are given.
Flow is conserved at every node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The formulation chooses installed arcs and feasible conserved flows; nonlinear arc costs or physical relations turn it into a nonconvex network-design MINLP.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-commodity bounded network design with nonlinear arc behavior.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Illustrative Applications of Global Optimization p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A network-design MINLP on a directed graph has the form \[\min\ \sum_{e}F_ez_e+\sum_e\phi_e(q_e)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bq=b,\quad \ell_ez_e\le q_e\le u_ez_e,\quad z_e\in\{0,1\}.\] The equation \(Bq=b\) enforces flow conservation, and the on-off bounds prohibit flow on uninstalled arcs. Additional node potentials and arc equations may be imposed. The model is nonconvex when some \(\phi_e\) is nonconvex on its flow interval or when an installed arc must satisfy a nonconvex relation among flow, potential, pressure, or loss variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network-design models choose arcs, enforce flow conservation and capacity activation, and become nonconvex through nonlinear costs or physical relations between flows and node potentials.

children.title: Spatial Layout Models
children.top_down_role: Geometric placement instances involving separation, overlap, or orientation constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Spatial Layout Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded placement models with discrete nonoverlap relations and potentially nonlinear geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a finite set of objects, let \(R\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a bounded placement region, and let \(u_i\) denote the position of object \(i\in\mathcal I\). For each pair \(i<j\), suppose nonoverlap is represented by the finite disjunction \[\bigvee_{r\in\mathcal R_{ij}}g_{ijr}(u_i,u_j)\le0.\] An exact indicator formulation introduces \(z_{ijr}\in\{0,1\}\) and imposes \[\sum_{r\in\mathcal R_{ij}}z_{ijr}=1,\qquad z_{ijr}=1\ \Longrightarrow\ g_{ijr}(u_i,u_j)\le0.\] Containment constraints require each placed object to lie inside \(R\), while additional discrete variables may select orientations. The objective may minimize occupied extent, connection cost, or weighted distance. Curved boundaries, Euclidean-distance equalities, and minimum-separation constraints can make the continuous relaxation nonconvex even after the discrete selections are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spatial-layout MINLP places finitely many objects in a bounded region, selects orientations or relative-position alternatives, and enforces containment and nonoverlap through linked binary indicators. Nonlinear geometry can make the continuous relaxation nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: A finite object set \(\mathcal I\) and a bounded placement region \(R\subset\mathbb R^d\) are given.
Each object has continuous position variables and finitely many permitted orientations or pairwise separation alternatives.
Every binary selector is linked to its selected geometric inequality by an exact indicator constraint or an equivalent valid formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution places every object inside the region and satisfies at least one valid nonoverlap relation for every object pair, together with the selected discrete spatial choices.

notation.meaning: binary selector for relative-position alternative r

children.title: Distance-Induced Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex structure arising from distance-dependent costs or feasibility conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Induced Nonconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean minimum-separation constraints in continuous location variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\ge1\), \(v\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(r>0\). The minimum-separation set \[S_{\ge}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\lVert u-v\rVert_2\ge r\}\] is nonconvex. Equivalently, the inequality \[r^2-\lVert u-v\rVert_2^2\le0\] defines a nonconvex feasible set. By contrast, the upper-distance set \[S_{\le}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\lVert u-v\rVert_2\le r\}\] is a convex Euclidean ball. Thus changing an upper distance bound to a positive lower separation bound crosses a convexity boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive lower bound on Euclidean distance defines a nonconvex minimum-separation set, whereas an upper distance bound defines a convex Euclidean ball.
assumptions_latex: The dimension satisfies \(d\ge1\).
The fixed center satisfies \(v\in\mathbb R^d\), and the separation radius satisfies \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lower-distance set \(S_{\ge}\) is nonconvex, while the upper-distance ball \(S_{\le}\) is convex.

children.title: Flow-Induced Nonconvexity
children.top_down_role: Nonconvex structure arising from nonlinear flow interactions.

assumptions_latex: A directed arc has positive coefficient \(k>0\), signed flow \(q\), and bounded nonnegative endpoint pressures.
The arc physics obey a steady-state pressure-drop relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow-pressure equality has a nonconvex feasible graph, and allowing flow reversal introduces an additional sign-dependent branch.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Steady-state bidirectional pressure-driven flow on one network arc.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Illustrative Applications of Global Optimization p. 4

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the arc relation \[q\lvert q\rvert=k(p_i^2-p_j^2),\qquad k>0.\] Even with fixed flow direction \(q\ge0\), it becomes \(q^2=k(p_i^2-p_j^2)\), an equality between convex quadratic expressions whose graph is generally nonconvex. With bidirectional flow, the law is the union of the branches \(q^2=k(p_i^2-p_j^2)\) for \(q\ge0\) and \(-q^2=k(p_i^2-p_j^2)\) for \(q\le0\). Binary installation or direction variables coupled to this law yield a nonconvex MINLP and require relaxations valid over bounded flow and pressure domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pressure-driven flow laws couple squared flow and pressure differences; their equality graph is nonconvex, and bidirectional operation adds distinct sign branches.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Induced Nonconvexity

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Illustrative Applications of Global Optimization p. 4

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical classification independent of any particular solver outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a benchmark MINLP, define its structure class by \[\kappa=(n_C,n_I,n_B,d,s),\] where \(n_C,n_I,n_B\) count continuous, general-integer, and binary variables; \(d\) is the largest total polynomial degree among objective and constraints when all expressions are polynomial, and \(d=\infty\) otherwise; and \(s\) records predicates such as quadratic, signomial, nonsmooth, equality-constrained, and sparse. A predicate is set only when it is established from the supplied domains and expression graph. The tuple \(\kappa\) describes formulation structure, not feasibility, boundedness, attainment, or whether a reported solution is globally optimal.

children.title: Benchmark Primal Evidence
children.top_down_role: Reference feasible points and best-known primal values.

assumptions_latex: A minimization benchmark has feasible set \(F\) and objective \(f:F\to\mathbb R\).
A candidate point is supplied with enough precision to evaluate every constraint and the objective under a stated tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A validated feasible point certifies an upper bound on the global optimum but does not by itself certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal evidence for minimization benchmarks under an explicit feasibility tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the exact feasible set of a minimization instance and \(f^*=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\). A primal certificate consists of a point \(\hat x\), its integer components, a feasibility tolerance \(\tau\), and reproducible evaluations showing that all variable-domain, equality, and inequality residuals satisfy the prescribed \(\tau\)-tests. If exact validation establishes \(\hat x\in F\), then \[f^*\le U:=f(\hat x).\] Among several validated points, the best-known primal value is the smallest corresponding \(U\). Feasibility and an objective value alone provide no lower bound and therefore do not establish global optimality unless matching dual or global-status evidence is also available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A validated feasible point supplies a primal objective value and hence an upper bound for minimization; the best-known primal value is the smallest such validated value.
knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Primal Evidence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact fact that a feasible point gives an upper bound for minimization is correct, but the record mixes tolerance-based residual validation with exact membership in the feasible set. A MINLPLib-specific source is needed to define its primal-value and feasibility-validation protocol before this can serve as a benchmark certificate record.

children.title: Benchmark Dual Evidence
children.top_down_role: Reference lower bounds and their provenance.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Dual Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate standard for reported lower bounds on minimization benchmarks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance with global value \(f^*\), benchmark dual evidence for a reported value \(L\) consists of a reproducible derivation establishing \(L\le f^*\). The evidence record shall identify the relaxation, dual construction, or exhaustive-search argument; all solver tolerances and relevant parameter settings; the computation time and software version; and any independently checkable certificate. A numerical value without a validity argument is only an observed bound, not certified dual evidence. Given a finite nonempty collection of valid bounds \(L_1,\ldots,L_m\), where \(m\in\mathbb N\), the benchmark bound is \(L_{\mathrm{ref}}=\max_{1\le j\le m}L_j\), with provenance retained for every contributing value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual evidence is a reproducible validity argument for a lower bound, including its method, tolerances, software, runtime, and any independently checkable certificate. For finitely many certified bounds, the reference bound is their maximum, with every provenance record retained.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a minimization problem with well-defined extended-real optimum \(f^*\).
\(m\in\mathbb N\) and \(m\ge1\).
Each bound \(L_j\), for \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), is finite and has a validity argument independent of the reported incumbent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{\mathrm{ref}}=\max_{1\le j\le m}L_j\le f^*\).

notation.meaning: global optimal value of the benchmark instance
certified lower bound from evidence item j

children.title: Benchmark Global-Status Evidence
children.top_down_role: Evidence supporting global-optimality and infeasibility classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Global-Status Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evidence predicates for globally optimal, globally infeasible, and unresolved benchmark statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization instance, a globally optimal status at tolerances \(\varepsilon_a,\varepsilon_r\ge0\) is certified by a feasible incumbent of value \(U\) and a valid lower bound \(L\) satisfying \(U-L\le \varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_r\max\{1,|U|\}\). Global infeasibility is certified only by a globally valid argument that the feasible set is empty, such as complete spatial enumeration with every node validly fathomed. If neither predicate is established, the global status is unresolved. Solver termination labels alone do not constitute benchmark global-status evidence unless their underlying certificates and tolerances are retained and validated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global optimality requires a feasible incumbent and matching valid bound; global infeasibility requires a valid emptiness certificate. Otherwise the benchmark remains unresolved.
assumptions_latex: \(L\le f^*\le U\) whenever a finite feasible incumbent and valid lower bound exist.
\(\varepsilon_a,\varepsilon_r\ge0\) are declared benchmark tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U-L\le\varepsilon_a+\varepsilon_r\max\{1,|U|\}\) certifies tolerance-global optimality; a valid emptiness argument certifies global infeasibility.

notation.meaning: objective value of a verified feasible incumbent

children.title: Primal–Dual Gap Trajectories
children.top_down_role: Time-dependent comparison of incumbent and valid-bound progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Trajectories
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone-envelope trajectory for incumbent and valid-bound progress in minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given timestamped feasible incumbent values \(U(s)\) and valid lower bounds \(L(s)\), define the monotone envelopes \(\bar U(t)=\inf_{0\le s\le t}U(s)\) and \(\bar L(t)=\sup_{0\le s\le t}L(s)\). When both are finite, the normalized primal–dual gap trajectory is \(g(t)=(\bar U(t)-\bar L(t))/\max\{1,|\bar U(t)|\}\); before both exist, set \(g(t)=+\infty\). Thus \(\bar U\) is nonincreasing, \(\bar L\) is nondecreasing, and \(g(t)\ge0\) whenever all recorded bounds are valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The trajectory compares the best incumbent and strongest valid bound available by each time, assigning infinite gap until both exist.
assumptions_latex: Every recorded incumbent is feasible.
Every recorded lower bound is globally valid for the minimization instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar U(t_2)\le\bar U(t_1)\), \(\bar L(t_2)\ge\bar L(t_1)\), and \(g(t)\ge0\) for \(t_2\ge t_1\).

notation.meaning: best incumbent value observed by time t
strongest valid lower bound observed by time t
normalized primal–dual gap at time t

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Size Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical distribution of processed-node counts across a fixed benchmark set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For benchmark set \(\mathcal I\) and solver configuration \(s\), let \(N_{i,s}\) be the number of search-tree nodes processed before certified termination or the resource limit on instance \(i\). The search-tree size profile is the empirical distribution \(F_s(n)=|\mathcal I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\mathbf 1\{N_{i,s}\le n\}\). Censored runs must additionally record the limit and censoring indicator; treating their observed node counts as completed-tree sizes is invalid. Comparisons require a common node-counting convention, including whether the root and reprocessed nodes are counted.

All configurations use the same node-counting convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Tree Shape Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Depth and width summaries of completed or censored global-search trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rooted search tree \(T_i=(V_i,E_i)\), define its width at depth \(d\) by \(w_i(d)=|\{v\in V_i:\operatorname{depth}(v)=d\}|\), maximum depth by \(D_i=\max_{v\in V_i}\operatorname{depth}(v)\), and normalized depth distribution by \(p_i(d)=w_i(d)/|V_i|\). A search-tree shape profile reports these quantities, or declared aggregates of them, across instances. For a resource-limited run the profile describes only the observed prefix tree and must be marked censored, because its maximum depth and width need not equal those of the eventual completed tree.

children.title: Relaxation Effort Profiles
children.top_down_role: Computational effort attributable to node relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Effort Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource profile for constructing and solving node relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instance \(i\), let \(K_i\) be the processed search nodes and let \(e_{ik}\ge0\) denote a declared relaxation resource at node \(k\), such as solve time, iterations, or oracle evaluations. Total relaxation effort is \(E_i=\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}e_{ik}\), and its cumulative share by search time \(t\) is \(R_i(t)=E_i^{-1}\sum_{k:\tau_{ik}\le t}e_{ik}\) when \(E_i>0\). A comparative profile must not combine distinct resource units and must separately identify relaxation construction, solution, and repeated-solve effort when available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation effort profiles aggregate a declared resource over processed nodes and show how that effort accumulates during search.
assumptions_latex: Every node effort \(e_{ik}\) is nonnegative and measured in one declared unit.
\(\tau_{ik}\) is the completion time associated with node effort \(e_{ik}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_i=\sum_{k=1}^{K_i}e_{ik}\), and \(R_i(t)\) is nondecreasing with values in \([0,1]\) when \(E_i>0\).

children.title: Relaxation Strength Profiles

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strength Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized bound improvement attributable to alternative valid relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization instance \(i\), let \(L_i^0\) be a baseline valid lower bound, \(L_i^r\) the valid bound from relaxation \(r\), and \(U_i\) a common feasible reference value with \(L_i^0\le L_i^r\le U_i\). When \(U_i>L_i^0\), define the relaxation-strength ratio \(S_i^r=(L_i^r-L_i^0)/(U_i-L_i^0)\). The profile of \(S_i^r\) over instances measures the fraction of the baseline primal–dual gap closed by \(r\). Instances with zero denominator and bounds violating the ordering are reported separately rather than assigned arbitrary ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation strength is the fraction of a common baseline gap closed by a stronger valid lower bound, profiled across instances.
assumptions_latex: \(L_i^0\le L_i^r\le U_i\).
\(U_i\) is the same feasible reference value for all compared relaxations on instance \(i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Tightening Cost–Benefit Profiles

children.title: Timeout Incidence Profiles
children.top_down_role: Frequency or distribution of runs terminated by time limits.

knowledge_statements.title: Timeout Incidence Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical timeout frequency as a function of the imposed time limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite benchmark set \(\mathcal I\), solver configuration \(s\), and time limit \(\tau\ge0\), let \(T_{i,s}\in[0,+\infty]\) be the time at which run \(i\) first attains the declared required terminal status, with \(T_{i,s}=+\infty\) if it never attains that status. Define \(Y_{i,s}(\tau)=\mathbf 1\{T_{i,s}>\tau\}\). The timeout incidence profile is \(q_s(\tau)=|\mathcal I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}Y_{i,s}(\tau)\), and it is nonincreasing in \(\tau\). Runs ending earlier through numerical failure must be classified separately unless the evaluation policy explicitly treats every unsuccessful termination as a timeout.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The timeout profile gives the benchmark fraction not reaching the required terminal status by each time limit, assigning infinite attainment time to runs that never reach it and separating earlier numerical failures unless policy says otherwise.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is a finite, nonempty, fixed benchmark set.
\(s\) is a fixed solver configuration.
The required terminal status and treatment of failures are declared before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le q_s(\tau)\le1\) and \(q_s(\tau_2)\le q_s(\tau_1)\) for \(\tau_2\ge\tau_1\ge0\).

notation.meaning: time to the required terminal status, or positive infinity if it is never attained

children.title: Numerical Failure Profiles
children.top_down_role: Frequency or distribution of numerically unsuccessful runs.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Failure Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical frequencies of declared numerical-failure categories.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix mutually exclusive numerical-failure categories \(\mathcal C\), such as invalid arithmetic, relaxation-solver failure, or unrecoverable feasibility-check failure. For instance \(i\) and solver configuration \(s\), let \(Z_{i,s}\in\mathcal C\cup\{\mathrm{none}\}\) be the first terminal numerical-failure category under a declared precedence rule. The category profile is \(p_s(c)=|\mathcal I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\mathbf 1\{Z_{i,s}=c\}\). Timeout, memory exhaustion, and unresolved optimality are not numerical failures unless explicitly included in \(\mathcal C\); logs must support every assigned category.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical-failure profile reports benchmark frequencies for predefined, mutually exclusive failure categories supported by execution logs.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is a finite, fixed benchmark set.
\(\mathcal C\) and the precedence rule are fixed before classifying runs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_s(c)\ge0\) and \(\sum_{c\in\mathcal C}p_s(c)\le1\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the failure-profile leaf and the category-frequency formula is correct. The failure taxonomy, precedence rule, and exclusions require an inspectable benchmark-policy source.

children.title: Status Consistency Profiles
children.top_down_role: Agreement of reported outcomes across repeated runs or solver configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Status Consistency Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise profile of compatibility between solver statuses and retained certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Map each validated run status to its mathematical assertion: optimal asserts a nonempty feasible set and an attained finite optimal value, infeasible asserts an empty feasible set, and unbounded-below asserts feasible points with arbitrarily small objective values. Two validated statuses are consistent only if their assertions can simultaneously hold for the same mathematical instance under the declared tolerances. Thus verified optimal and verified infeasible statuses are inconsistent, verified optimal and verified unbounded-below statuses are inconsistent, and verified infeasible and verified unbounded-below statuses are inconsistent. For a finite nonempty benchmark set \(\mathcal I\) and configurations \(r\) and \(s\), define \(C_{r,s}=|\mathcal I|^{-1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\mathbf 1\{\text{the validated assertions of configurations }r\text{ and }s\text{ on }i\text{ are compatible}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A status-consistency profile is the fraction of benchmark instances for which two configurations' certificate-backed assertions can simultaneously hold under common tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) is a finite, nonempty, common benchmark instance set.
All compared runs use mathematically identical instances and common status tolerances.
Statuses are interpreted through retained, validated assertions rather than labels alone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le C_{r,s}\le1\), and each pair of contradictory validated optimality, infeasibility, or unbounded-below assertions contributes \(0\).

notation.meaning: common finite nonempty benchmark instance set

children.title: Unresolved Instance Profiles
children.top_down_role: Instances lacking a conclusive feasible, infeasible, or optimal status.

knowledge_statements.title: Unresolved Instance Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical profile of benchmark instances lacking a conclusive global-solver outcome by a fixed resource limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite benchmark set, let \(R_i\) be the attempted runs on instance \(i\), and let \(c(r)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether run \(r\) terminates with a validated global-optimal, infeasible, or unbounded certificate. For a feature map \(\phi:I\to\mathcal X\) and bin \(B\subseteq\mathcal X\), define the unresolved-instance profile by \[U(B)=\frac{\left|\left\{i\in I:\phi(i)\in B,\ \sum_{r\in R_i}c(r)=0\right\}\right|}{\left|\left\{i\in I:\phi(i)\in B\right\}\right|}.\] The ratio is undefined when its denominator is zero; unresolved runs must retain their terminal status, resource use, and best bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each instance-feature bin, the profile reports the fraction of instances for which no attempted run produced a validated conclusive certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and every \(R_i\) are finite.
All runs use a fixed validation rule and resource limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U(B)\in[0,1]\) whenever \(\left|\{i\in I:\phi(i)\in B\}\right|>0\).

notation.meaning: indicator of a validated conclusive result
unresolved-instance rate in feature bin B

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the unresolved-instance profile container and is internally coherent, but no citation supports the particular instance-level aggregation or the classification of global-optimal, infeasible, and unbounded outcomes as validated conclusive certificates. The listed local sources do not address this benchmarking protocol.

children.title: Perturbation Sensitivity Profiles
children.top_down_role: Outcome variation under small changes to data or computational settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Sensitivity Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reliability profile under controlled, semantics-preserving or explicitly quantified perturbations of benchmark data and run conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each benchmark instance \(i\in I\), let \(P_i(\delta)\) be a finite family of perturbations of magnitude at most \(\delta\), including the unperturbed run, and let \(y_{ip}=(s_{ip},v_{ip},L_{ip},U_{ip})\) record status, incumbent value, and final bounds. Given a declared discrepancy predicate \(D(y_{ip},y_{i0})\), define \[S(\delta)=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i\in I}\frac{1}{|P_i(\delta)|-1}\sum_{p\in P_i(\delta)\setminus\{0\}}\mathbf 1\{D(y_{ip},y_{i0})\}.\] The perturbation sensitivity profile is the function \(\delta\mapsto S(\delta)\), reported together with the perturbation generator and discrepancy tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile maps perturbation magnitude to the average fraction of perturbed runs whose status, objective, or bounds materially differ from the baseline.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and \(|P_i(\delta)|\ge 2\) for every evaluated \(i\).
Baseline and perturbed runs share all controls not designated for perturbation.

notation.meaning: controlled perturbations of instance i up to magnitude delta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the perturbation-sensitivity container, and its notation and range claim are coherent. An authoritative source is required for the nested averaging formula, treatment of perturbation magnitude, and use of the protocol-dependent discrepancy predicate; the local inventory does not support these choices.

children.title: Computational Reproducibility Controls
children.top_down_role: Control of solver versions, model transformations, tolerances, hardware, and run conditions.

children.title: Solver Version Control
children.top_down_role: Recording solver releases, component versions, or build identifiers.

knowledge_statements.title: Solver Version Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducibility condition fixing the executable identity and software stack used in a computational comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E(r)=(n,v,b,h,d)\) denote the solver environment of run \(r\): solver name, semantic version, build identifier, executable digest, and dependency manifest. Solver version control holds for a run set \(R\) precisely when either \[E(r)=E(r')\quad\text{for all }r,r'\in R,\] or every distinct environment is declared as a separate experimental treatment. The archived record must identify \(E(r)\), solver options whose defaults depend on the version, and any local patches. Reproduction requires selecting an environment with the recorded executable digest or documenting a version deviation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runs are version-controlled when they use one fully identified solver build, or when differing builds are treated and reported as separate experiments.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is the set of runs intended to share one solver treatment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Environment-dependent solver changes are not confounded with the treatment represented by \(R\).

notation.meaning: runs assigned to one solver treatment
recorded solver environment for run r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind and statement fit Solver Version Control, but the asserted necessary metadata, separation rule, and executable-digest reproduction requirement are uncited protocol prescriptions. None of the inventoried sources specifically supports them.

children.title: Model Transformation Control
children.top_down_role: Recording presolve, reformulation, scaling, or conversion choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Model Transformation Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducibility condition fixing preprocessing, reformulation, scaling, and generated solver-input models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M_i\) be the declared source model for instance \(i\), and let \(T_	heta\) be the complete transformation pipeline with configuration \(\theta\). Model transformation control holds when every compared run assigned to the same transformation treatment receives \(\widehat M_i=T_	heta(M_i)\), and the source digest, ordered transformations, parameter values, software versions, and digest of \(\widehat M_i\) are recorded. If two treatments use \(T_	heta\) and \(T_{	heta'}\), they must be reported separately. Any claim that a transformation preserves feasibility or optimal values must state and check the corresponding variable and objective mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A controlled experiment fixes and records the complete model-transformation pipeline and generated model, separating runs that use different transformations.
assumptions_latex: Each source model \(M_i\) has a stable archived representation.
The configured pipeline \(T_\theta\) is deterministic, or its random state is recorded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All runs within one transformation treatment receive an auditable common transformed model \(\widehat M_i\).

notation.meaning: source model for benchmark instance i
solver-input model produced by the pipeline

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Model Transformation Control and is mathematically coherent, but its required audit fields and its feasibility and objective-mapping checks are substantive protocol choices without supporting citations. The available global-optimization sources do not establish this reproducibility standard.

children.title: Tolerance Configuration Control
children.top_down_role: Recording feasibility, optimality, integrality, or termination tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Configuration Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducibility condition fixing feasibility, integrality, optimality, gap, and numerical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau(r)=(\tau_f,\tau_I,\tau_o,\tau_a,\tau_r,\tau_n)\) collect the feasibility, integrality, optimality, absolute-gap, relative-gap, and numerical tolerances applied in run \(r\). Tolerance configuration control holds for a treatment \(R\) when \[\tau(r)=\tau(r')\quad\text{for all }r,r'\in R,\] with every component's definition, units, stopping role, and effective value recorded. Solver defaults count as values and must be resolved against the recorded solver version. Runs using different tolerance vectors constitute separate treatments unless tolerance is the explicit experimental factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comparable runs use the same fully recorded tolerance vector; differing tolerances are isolated as an explicit experimental factor.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) contains runs intended to share one tolerance treatment.
Each effective tolerance can be recovered from configuration and solver-version metadata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tolerance-induced differences are excluded within \(R\) or explicitly represented between treatments.

notation.meaning: runs assigned to one tolerance treatment
effective tolerance vector for run r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Tolerance Configuration Control, but the tolerance vector is not solver-independent: feasibility, optimality, gap, and generic numerical tolerances can have different definitions and roles across solvers. A source or declared benchmarking standard is needed to support the components and comparison rule.

children.title: Hardware Environment Control
children.top_down_role: Recording computational resources relevant to benchmark comparability.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardware Environment Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducibility condition fixing or stratifying computational hardware and its resource allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H(r)=(c,a,m,g,o,q)\) record the processor model, instruction architecture, available memory, accelerator configuration, operating-system environment, and allocated thread or core quota for run \(r\). Hardware environment control holds for a run treatment \(R\) when either \[H(r)=H(r')\quad\text{for all }r,r'\in R,\] or each distinct hardware environment is a declared block in the analysis. Clock-management policy, simultaneous workloads, virtualization, affinity, and resource limits must also be recorded whenever elapsed time, energy, or numerical reproducibility is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Runs share a documented hardware allocation, or hardware differences are explicitly blocked so performance and reliability comparisons are not confounded.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) contains runs whose resource measurements are compared.
Hardware metadata are collected at execution time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hardware variation is held constant within \(R\) or represented as an explicit analysis factor.

notation.meaning: runs assigned to one hardware treatment or block
recorded hardware environment for run r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Hardware Environment Control, but the equality or blocking rule and the enumerated mandatory metadata are uncited experimental-design prescriptions whose relevance depends on the measured outcomes. The local sources do not substantiate this protocol.

children.title: Run Condition Control
children.top_down_role: Recording limits, random seeds, parallelism settings, or execution conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Run Condition Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reproducibility condition fixing per-run initialization, limits, scheduling, and execution policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(r)=(s,t,m,k,p,o)\) denote the run conditions for run \(r\): random seed or stream, time limit, memory limit, thread count, scheduling policy, and execution order. Run condition control holds for a treatment \(R\) when \(C(r)\) follows one predeclared protocol for every \(r\in R\). Fixed factors must be equal; randomized or blocked factors must be generated by the recorded design. Restarts, warm starts, concurrent jobs, termination signals, and failed-run handling must be specified before aggregation, and every deviation must be retained in the run log.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every run follows a predeclared execution protocol, with fixed conditions matched and randomized or blocked conditions generated by the recorded design.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is the run set governed by one experimental protocol.
Protocol deviations and incomplete runs are retained rather than silently discarded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each observed outcome in \(R\) is associated with an auditable condition vector \(C(r)\).

notation.meaning: runs governed by one experimental protocol

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits Run Condition Control and is internally consistent, but the prescribed condition vector, preaggregation requirements, and deviation-retention rule require an authoritative computational-experiment or benchmarking source. The inventoried sources do not support these specific requirements.
